## Decisions & candidate options

### d1 Carrier status ingestion: webhook push vs status API polling vs hybrid
Settled input: C-1 (weigh both, pick the simplest meeting PRD p95 < 300 ms) and C-2 (shared secret per carrier), from the run prompt in requirements.md "Prompt" section, items (1) and (2). Both carriers support signed webhook push and status API polling (same source).

Evidence:
- AC-2: "Carrier status changes reach the shop within a minute of the carrier recording them" (requirements.md, Acceptance criteria).
- NFR1: "p95 API latency under 300 ms" (docs/product/prd.md line 28, as cited in authoring-scope.md Analysis); G2 99.9% availability (prd.md line 17).
- Repo: `git ls-files` lists only src/shop/__init__.py and tests/test_health.py under code. Per authoring-scope.md Analysis, src has only `PAGE_SIZE`, `health()`, `list_customers()`; pyproject.toml has no dependencies. So there is no scheduler, worker, HTTP framework, persistence or carrier client. Any option adds its runtime from nothing; the question is which adds less.

#### Option A: webhook push (preliminary winner)
How it works: each carrier POSTs a signed callback to one receiver route (proposed `POST /carriers/{carrier}/webhooks`). The handler reads the raw body, verifies the per-carrier HMAC and timestamp (d4, C-2), normalises the payload through a carrier adapter, writes the event and projection in one transaction (d2) and acks 2xx.
- AC-2: end-to-end latency is carrier send time plus our handler, typically seconds. Margin against 60 s is large. Carrier retry policy affects only failure cases (assumption A-D1-1 below).
- NFR1: handler does one HMAC check and one DB transaction, with no outbound calls (email is off-path per d3). This is bounded work, so p95 < 300 ms is plausible. Needs a load test (S5 in scope rollout).
- Simplicity: no scheduler, no per-order polling state, no carrier rate-limit management, no carrier credentials for outbound calls. Only a route and a verifier.
- Availability: carriers retry while we are down for short outages. Long outages leave status stale; no self-healing (see Option C).
- Security: public inbound endpoint. Needs raw-body HMAC, replay window, constant-time compare, body-size cap, rate limit.
- Cons: duplicates and out-of-order delivery need idempotency (unique carrier + carrier_event_id, occurred_at comparison, d2).

#### Option B: status API polling
How it works: a scheduled job iterates open shipments per carrier, calls the carrier status API, diffs against the stored status and records changes.
- AC-2: worst-case latency is roughly poll interval + call duration + processing. To keep a safety margin under 60 s the interval must be about 30 s or less. Each open shipment is then polled about twice a minute per carrier, unless a carrier offers a bulk or since-cursor endpoint (unverified, assumption A-D1-2). Call volume grows linearly with open orders; rate limits and per-call costs are unknown.
- NFR1: the poller is not on a user-facing request path, so p95 of shopper endpoints is not directly affected. It does compete for DB and CPU with them.
- Simplicity: no inbound surface and no signature handling, but needs a scheduler/worker process, outbound carrier credentials, rate-limit and backoff logic and per-carrier clients. None of this exists in src.
- Availability: self-healing after our downtime (next poll catches up). But a carrier API outage stalls ingestion, and a long poll cycle can itself breach AC-2.
- Cons: wasted calls when nothing changed; more infra; tight coupling of AC-2 to cron cadence.

#### Option C: hybrid (webhook primary plus low-frequency reconciliation poll)
How it works: Option A plus a slow poll (for example every 5-15 min, only for open shipments with no recent event) to repair missed callbacks.
- Pros: closes the missed-callback gap and the long-outage availability concern against G2.
- Cons: needs everything Option B needs (scheduler, outbound clients, credentials) in addition to Option A, so it is strictly more than the simplest option. Fails C-1 "simplest" for the first release.
- Disposition: rejected for release 1, recorded as optional follow-up slice S6. It can share the outbox drain loop slot from d3 as the first background process, so adding it later is additive and does not change the handler or data model (event dedupe key makes polled and pushed events converge).

#### Recommendation
Option A. It is the simplest option that meets AC-2 with margin and NFR1 (C-1), requires no new scheduling infrastructure and authenticates with a per-carrier shared secret as C-2 allows. Option C stays as a documented, additive follow-up; the main residual risk (missed callbacks) is mitigated by carrier retries, an idempotent handler, and a stale-open-shipment alert.

Assumptions (recorded, because the user cannot answer):
- A-D1-1: both carriers retry non-2xx callbacks with backoff for a bounded window. Not verified; confirm in carrier docs when building the adapters (consistent with authoring-scope A-2).
- A-D1-2: carrier polling APIs have no bulk/since-cursor guarantee, so per-shipment polling cost is assumed for Option B. If a bulk endpoint exists, Option B's cost drops but infra need remains.
- A-D1-3: p95 < 300 ms applies to the webhook receiver as an API endpoint; the handler budget is verify + one transaction. Verified by load test, not by this design.

Single decision, not single-option: A and B are both viable, so no strawman.

## Open questions

- None blocking. C-1 and C-2 settle the choice criteria and the authentication model.
- To confirm at implementation (not asked, user cannot answer): carrier retry/backoff policy and delivery guarantees (A-D1-1), signature header/algorithm per carrier (authoring-scope A-2), existence of bulk status endpoints (A-D1-2).
- Team may choose at review whether S6 reconciliation poll ships with release 1 given G2 99.9%; default is follow-up.

## Risks

- Missed callbacks during our downtime or carrier-side loss leave status stale and breach AC-2 for those orders. Mitigation: carrier retries, idempotent handler, alert on open shipments with no event beyond a threshold, follow-up S6 reconciliation poll. Wrong-decision cost: low, because the poll is additive.
- Public inbound endpoint is an attack surface. Mitigation: per-carrier HMAC with timestamp window, constant-time compare, 401 without detail, body-size cap, rate limit, no secret/signature logging, rotation by accepting current+previous secret.
- Duplicate and out-of-order callbacks. Mitigation: unique (carrier, carrier_event_id), compare occurred_at before moving current_status (d2).
- Carrier retry policy unknown (A-D1-1): if retries are absent or short, push loses events during outages and Option C moves from optional to required. Early check in S3.
- NFR1 not proven by design: handler p95 under 300 ms needs a load test in S5.
- Wrong-decision blast radius: confined to the receiver route and carrier adapters; the data model and email path are independent of how events arrive.

## Decisions & candidate options

### d2 Status data model (research slice; refines scope notes d2, authoring-scope.md lines 19-22)

Drivers: AC-1 (current status AND history per order, requirements.md "Acceptance criteria"); idempotency and out-of-order carrier callbacks (d1 picks webhook push, so carriers retry and reorder; authoring-scope.md line 14); NFR1 p95 < 300 ms (docs/product/prd.md:28, as cited in scope notes line 5); AC-3 needs one email per status change, with an outbox row written in the same transaction (d3, scope line 26). Code evidence: src/shop/__init__.py (lines 1-9 per scope notes) has no persistence and no order model, so every option is greenfield and the orders table is owned by checkout (F2); the design only adds a FK to it (assumption A-5, scope line 90).

#### Option A: append-only event table + orders.current_status projection, same transaction (recommended)
- How it works: `order_status_event(id, order_id FK, carrier, carrier_event_id, status, occurred_at, received_at, raw_payload_ref)`, UNIQUE(carrier, carrier_event_id), INDEX(order_id, occurred_at). `orders` gains `current_status` and `current_status_at`. Handler, in one transaction: INSERT event ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING; if 0 rows inserted it is a duplicate, so commit and ack 200 with no further effect (no second email). Otherwise UPDATE orders SET current_status, current_status_at WHERE id = ? AND (current_status_at IS NULL OR current_status_at < :occurred_at) (tie-break on event id); and INSERT email_outbox keyed by event id. The email decision is made on the status change event, not on projection movement (see Open questions Q1).
- Idempotency: DB-enforced via the unique key, so concurrent duplicate deliveries are safe without locks.
- Out-of-order: late event is still stored (history complete, AC-1) but cannot regress the projection, since the guarded UPDATE is conditional on occurred_at. History reads order by occurred_at, not received_at.
- AC-1: history = `SELECT ... WHERE order_id=? ORDER BY occurred_at`; current status = single column read. Order list page reads orders.current_status with no join, which protects NFR1 on list views.
- NFR1: write path is 1 INSERT + 1 conditional UPDATE + 1 outbox INSERT in one local transaction, no outbound calls: well under 300 ms.
- Cons: two sources of truth; projection can drift if any code path writes events without the projection. Mitigation: a single repository function is the only writer (module src/shop/tracking/), plus a consistency check query (current_status equals latest event) in tests and an ops job; projection is rebuildable from events at any time.
- Cost: storage grows by a few rows per order (6 normalised statuses, scope A-4); negligible.

#### Option B: derive-on-read, events only (no projection)
- How it works: same event table and unique key; current status = latest event by occurred_at (`ORDER BY occurred_at DESC LIMIT 1`, or a lateral join for lists). No orders column.
- Pros: one write, no drift by construction, nothing to rebuild; idempotency and history identical to A.
- Cons: every order list needs a latest-per-order lookup; with the (order_id, occurred_at) index this is cheap for one order but a per-row lateral join on a page of orders is a larger NFR1 risk and couples checkout/order queries to the tracking table. The "did status change" decision for AC-3 needs a read of the previous latest event inside the transaction (a lock or serialisable read is needed to avoid two concurrent callbacks both deciding they changed it). Marginally weaker under concurrency than A's conditional UPDATE.
- Viability: genuinely viable at small scale; scale is not quantified in the PRD (assumption, see Risks).

#### Option C: single mutable orders.status column, overwritten
- How it works: callback overwrites the column.
- Fails AC-1 (no history) and has no dedupe key, so duplicates cannot be told from changes (AC-3 would double-send), and an out-of-order callback regresses the status. Rejected as non-viable against requirements; listed for completeness, not a strawman for the choice between A and B.

#### Option D (variant of A, noted): materialised view or cache of the latest event instead of a column
- Rejected: adds refresh lag against AC-2 and operational complexity for no gain over a column updated in-transaction.

### Preliminary recommendation
Option A. It meets AC-1 with a trivial history query, gives DB-enforced idempotency, handles out-of-order without losing data, keeps list reads flat for NFR1, and the projection is always rebuildable from the log, which removes most of its drift risk. Fall back to Option B only if the team wants to avoid adding columns to the checkout-owned orders table (see Q2); the event table and handler contract are identical, so the switch is cheap.

## Open questions

No user input needed (user cannot answer; recorded as assumptions/decisions for the review):
- Q1 (assumption D2-1): Does a delayed (older occurred_at) event that does not move current_status still trigger an email? Proposed: no email, because the shopper-visible status did not change; history still records it. AC-3 reads "every order status change", which this satisfies, but the team may prefer an email for any stored event. Settle at review.
- Q2 (assumption D2-2): Adding `current_status` and `current_status_at` to `orders` requires coordination with checkout (F2), which owns that table and does not exist yet (scope G-3). Proposed: tracking owns the two columns via its own migration in slice S1; if orders is not ready, S1 creates a minimal stub per the scope rollout.
- Q3 (assumption D2-3): Event ordering key is the carrier's `occurred_at`; carriers are assumed to provide a timestamp and a stable event id in the signed payload (scope A-2). If a carrier lacks an event id, fall back to a hash of (order, status, occurred_at) as the dedupe key; confirm at carrier-adapter implementation (S3).
- Q4 (assumption D2-4): Status transitions are not required to be strictly monotonic (e.g. exception then in_transit allowed); the projection follows latest-by-occurred_at, not a state-machine order. Confirm against carrier docs (scope A-4).
- Q5: The initial `paid` event is produced by checkout (F2) or by S1 seeding, not by a carrier; it has carrier = 'shop' and a synthetic event id (the order id). Assumption pending F2 design.

- Projection drift (A): any second writer of orders.current_status breaks the invariant. Mitigation: single writer function, same-transaction update, invariant test, rebuild-from-events script. Wrong-decision cost: low (events remain the truth).
- Timestamp ties or clock skew from carriers: equal or skewed occurred_at could pick the wrong "latest". Mitigation: tie-break by event id/received_at; use history ordering by (occurred_at, id); log projections that did not move for diagnosis.
- Row contention on a hot order (concurrent callbacks): the conditional UPDATE serialises per order row; acceptable at per-order rates (a handful of events per order).
- Dependency on checkout-owned orders table (Q2): schema coordination; blast radius is one migration touching a table that does not yet exist in code (src/shop/__init__.py has no persistence).
- Unknown scale (volume of orders and events not in the PRD as read in scope notes): assumed modest; Option B's list-read cost and Option A's write amplification would both be re-checked in the S5 load test against NFR1.
- Raw payload retention may include personal data (shipping address): store a reference or minimised payload only (scope NFR checklist, compliance note line 39).
- Backfill: orders existing before rollout have no events; S1 seeds one event per order from its current known state, or leaves history empty with current_status null (displayed as "processing"); decide at S1.

- Confirm the email-on-change rule (Q1) and orders-table ownership (Q2) are stated as assumptions in the draft Open questions.

## Decisions & candidate options

### d4 Callback authentication for carrier webhooks (settled input: C-2 callbacks authenticated, shared secret per carrier acceptable; requirements.md Prompt item 2)

Evidence read: requirements.md (Prompt items 1-2: both carriers "support signed webhook push"; AC-2 within a minute); authoring-scope.md (## Decisions d4 lines 30-33, NFR checklist Security line 37, d2 unique (carrier, carrier_event_id) line 20, Risks "Secret leakage/rotation" line 97, A-2 line 90). Code reality from scope notes: src/shop/__init__.py lines 1-9 is a stub and pyproject.toml has no dependencies, so any option should use the Python standard library only (`hmac`, `hashlib`, `secrets`); I did not re-open src in this slice.

Shared facts for both options:
- Endpoint is `POST /carriers/{carrier}/webhooks` (scope d1 option A). The `{carrier}` path segment selects which secret to use; an unknown carrier gets 404 with no secret lookup.
- Failure response is a uniform 401 that does not reveal which check failed (scope NFR Security line 37). Verification runs BEFORE any parsing or DB write, so an unauthenticated caller costs one HMAC/compare, and the NFR1 p95 < 300 ms budget (prd.md:28 per scope line 5) is not at risk.
- Replay: d2 already makes the handler idempotent via unique (carrier, carrier_event_id), so a replayed valid body creates no second event and no second email (d3 outbox row is written in the same transaction). The auth layer therefore only needs to bound replay, not eliminate it.

#### Option A: HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body plus timestamp (recommended)
How it works: carrier sends `X-Signature` (hex or base64 HMAC-SHA256) and `X-Timestamp`. Shop computes HMAC over `timestamp + "." + raw_body` with the carrier's secret, compares with `hmac.compare_digest`, and rejects when |now - timestamp| exceeds a tolerance (proposed 5 minutes, configurable). Raw bytes must be captured before JSON parsing. Rotation: each carrier has an ordered list of at most two secrets (current, previous); verification tries both, so the carrier can switch on its own schedule; remove the previous secret after the overlap window.
Pros: secret never on the wire; body integrity (tampering of status, order or tracking number is detected); replay bounded by the timestamp window and made harmless by d2 dedupe; matches the brief that both carriers "support signed webhook push", so no carrier-side extra work; stdlib only, so no new dependency; rotation without downtime.
Cons: raw-body access is needed (framework choice is undecided, A-1; must be a requirement on the HTTP layer); depends on carrier signature scheme (exact header names, encoding, whether timestamp is signed; A-2); clock skew between carrier and shop can cause false rejects (mitigated by tolerance and NTP); a carrier that re-sends retries with the ORIGINAL timestamp could be rejected after the window, losing events (see Risks).
Implementation cost: low-moderate; one pure function `verify_signature(secret_list, headers, raw_body, now)` per carrier adapter, trivially unit-testable (supports NFR2 >= 90%, scope line 40).

#### Option B: static shared token in a header, constant-time compare
How it works: carrier sends `Authorization: Bearer <token>` or `X-Carrier-Token`; shop compares against the per-carrier token with `hmac.compare_digest` over TLS. Rotation: accept current+previous token.
Pros: simplest to build and to configure on the carrier side; no raw-body capture, no clock dependency; works even if a carrier's signing is awkward.
Cons: the secret is sent on every request, so any TLS-terminating proxy, access log or APM tool that captures headers leaks it (scope Security line 37 already forbids logging secrets, which is harder to enforce for headers); no integrity (a valid token authorises any body); fully replayable by anyone who observes one request, so replay is limited only by d2 dedupe, and a captured token allows forging NEW events with fresh event ids; does not use the signed push capability the carriers already offer.
Implementation cost: lowest, but the saving over A is small (about one function), so it does not buy much.

#### Option C (considered, not a standalone choice): network controls only (mTLS or carrier IP allowlist)
Stronger transport identity if both carriers offer mTLS or fixed egress IPs, but this is unconfirmed (no source says so), adds certificate or ingress operations that do not exist (no hld/deployment.md per scope line 45), and does not satisfy C-2's "shared secret per carrier" framing. Recorded as an optional defence-in-depth layer at the edge, not as the application-level decision.

#### Comparison against criteria
| Criterion | A: HMAC + timestamp | B: static token |
|---|---|---|
| Security (C-2, NFR) | Authenticity + integrity, secret not sent | Authenticity only, secret sent each call |
| Replay | Bounded by window, harmless via d2 | Unbounded, only d2 dedupe |
| Rotation | Current+previous secret overlap | Current+previous token overlap |
| Compromise via logs/proxy | Signature is single-use-ish, secret not exposed | Token exposed, forgery possible |
| Implementation cost | Low-moderate, stdlib | Lowest, stdlib |
| Dependency on carrier | Needs signed push (stated available) | Needs custom header support (assumed) |
| Perf impact (NFR1) | One HMAC over small body, negligible | Negligible |

#### Recommendation for d4
Option A. B loses on the security NFR for a marginal saving, and the carriers' signed push is stated as available (requirements.md Prompt item 1). Concrete parameters to put in the draft: per-carrier secret list in env/secret store (never in repo or logs), constant-time compare, 5-minute tolerance (proposal, tunable), uniform 401, 64 KiB body cap checked before hashing (proposal), metrics `callbacks_rejected{reason}` with the reason kept in metrics/internal logs only, not in the response. Fall back to B only for a carrier that proves unable to sign, as a per-carrier adapter setting, and then require TLS plus the edge controls from Option C; that fallback is itself a risk acceptance for the team to note at review.

Assumptions (flagged, user cannot answer; confirm in the carrier adapter slice S3):
- A-2 (carried from scope): exact header names, digest encoding, signed string layout and timestamp semantics per carrier come from carrier docs, not from anything in the repo.
- A-d4-1: carriers re-sign each retry with a fresh timestamp. If a carrier retries with the original timestamp, set the tolerance above its maximum retry horizon, because d2 idempotency makes a wide window safe.
- A-d4-2: each carrier can hold two secrets or can switch at an agreed time, so overlap-based rotation works; if not, rotation needs a short agreed maintenance window.
- A-d4-3: the HTTP layer (undecided, A-1) can expose the unparsed request body.

## Open questions

- None that block the design; the user cannot answer and C-2 settles that a per-carrier shared secret is acceptable.
- For the team at review (non-blocking, each with its options): (1) timestamp tolerance, 5 min (proposed) vs 1 min (tighter, risks skew false rejects against AC-2); (2) whether to add the edge-level IP allowlist or mTLS (Option C) as defence-in-depth, yes/no, depends on carrier support and the deployment view that does not yet exist.
- Ledger: C-2 (settled); A-2, A-d4-1..3 are assumptions, not ledger entries.

## Risks

- Carrier signature scheme differs from the assumed layout (A-2): wrong assumption means rejecting all genuine callbacks, which breaks AC-2 completely. Mitigation: per-carrier verifier in the adapter, contract tests with carrier-published sample payloads, a staging run before the flag is enabled (rollout slice S3 behind `order_tracking_enabled`). Wrong-decision cost is low: only the adapter function changes.
- Rejected genuine retries because of the timestamp window or clock skew (A-d4-1): events lost until the carrier retries again, AC-2 breach. Mitigation: tolerance wide enough because d2 dedupe makes replay harmless; NTP on hosts; alert on spike of `callbacks_rejected{reason=timestamp}`.
- Secret leakage or poor rotation (scope Risks line 97): per-carrier secrets, overlap rotation, never logged, never in the repo; rotation runbook belongs in the docs-sync output.
- Raw-body requirement is violated by a framework middleware that re-serialises JSON: signature always fails or, worse, devs "fix" it by verifying the parsed body. Mitigation: LLD/API note requiring verification on the raw bytes plus a unit test using a body with unusual whitespace and key order.
- Unauthenticated traffic on a public endpoint (DoS): body-size cap and rate limiting at the edge (S5), verification is cheap and happens first.
- Fallback to static token (Option B) for a carrier that cannot sign would weaken security: needs an explicit risk acceptance by the team and is recorded as an exception, not the default.
- Blast radius of this decision: only the carrier webhook receiver (scope slice S3) and the secret configuration; nothing in src/ exists yet to change.

## Reviewer checklist (d4 slice)

- Confirm the draft marks A-2 and A-d4-1..3 as assumptions and does not invent a carrier header name as fact.
- Confirm the 401 response is uniform and no secret or signature is logged.
ACS_EOF

## Decisions & candidate options

### d3 Email on every status change (AC-3): synchronous vs transactional outbox vs fire-and-forget

Evidence read: requirements.md (AC-3 "emailed on every order status change"; prompt answer 3: outbound transactional email API, provider undecided, does not change the design); authoring-scope.md d1-d3 and NFR checklist (NFR1 p95 < 300 ms from docs/product/prd.md:28 as cited there; G2 99.9%, prd.md:17); code reality per scope notes (src/shop/__init__.py lines 1-9: no framework, no persistence, no email, no background process; pyproject.toml has no dependencies). I did not re-open the PRD or src files in this slice; those citations are inherited from the scope notes.

Constraints that frame the choice:
- AC-3 says "every" status change: a lost email is a requirement violation, so the delivery guarantee must be at-least-once with dedupe, not best-effort.
- NFR1 p95 < 300 ms applies to the webhook handler (d1 pick A) and the shopper endpoints. Handler is meant to be verify + one DB transaction (scope d1). A third-party call inside it puts provider latency into the p95.
- C-3: provider unknown, so the design needs a provider-agnostic `EmailSender` port.
- Carriers retry on non-2xx or timeout (assumption A-6 below). A handler that blocks on or fails because of the email API turns a mail outage into duplicate carrier callbacks.
- Operability: shop has no background process today and no deployment view (scope Architecture conformance call), so any new worker is new infra.

#### Option A: synchronous send inside the webhook handler
How it works: after verifying and persisting the event, the handler calls `EmailSender.send()` and only then returns 2xx.
- Pros: fewest moving parts, no worker, no extra table; email is sent at once.
- Cons: provider latency adds directly to handler latency, so NFR1 p95 depends on a third party (typical transactional APIs are 100-500 ms per call, an assumption, not measured here, so one call alone can exceed the 300 ms budget). Provider failure forces a choice: fail the callback (carrier retries, duplicates, the event is already committed so dedupe must absorb it, and the email is still not guaranteed) or swallow the error (email lost, violating AC-3). Cannot retry with backoff without holding the carrier connection. Couples availability (G2) of ingestion to the email provider.
- Verdict: fails NFR1 risk and AC-3 reliability. Viable only as a prototype.

#### Option B: transactional outbox with an async sender
How it works: in the same DB transaction that inserts the `order_status_event` and moves `orders.current_status`, the handler inserts one `email_outbox` row (columns proposed: id, event_id UNIQUE, order_id, recipient reference, status in pending/sent/failed/dead, attempts, next_attempt_at, created_at, sent_at, last_error). The handler returns 2xx after commit with no outbound call. A sender drains rows `WHERE status='pending' AND next_attempt_at <= now()` (claimed with row locking, e.g. `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, or an equivalent atomic claim, depending on the DB chosen, A-1), calls `EmailSender.send(idempotency_key=event_id)`, and marks sent; on error it increments attempts and sets `next_attempt_at` with exponential backoff, moving to `dead` after a cap (alerted).
- Pros: handler stays DB-only, protecting NFR1; the email intent is committed atomically with the status change, so no status change can exist without a pending email (AC-3 "every"); retries survive crashes and provider outages; unique(event_id) plus the provider idempotency key gives effectively-once sending; unique(event_id) also makes a duplicate carrier callback (already deduped on carrier_event_id in d2) unable to enqueue a second email; adds natural metrics (outbox depth, oldest pending age). The same drain loop can later host the reconciliation poll (scope d1 option C).
- Cons: new background component; one more table; delivery latency is the drain interval plus send time (poll interval proposal 1-5 s, or wake-on-insert signal, so email lands well within a minute; this is a proposed internal target, not a requirement); at-least-once means a crash between provider accept and `mark sent` can double-send unless the provider honours the idempotency key (assumption A-7), otherwise a rare duplicate email is accepted.
- Sub-choice B1, in-process drain loop (thread/async task started with the app): simplest deploy, no new process type; with several app replicas it needs the row-claim lock above, and a stuck app stops sending. Sub-choice B2, separate worker process: independent scaling and failure isolation, but needs a second deployable that deployment docs do not define yet. Recommendation: build the drain as a plain function `drain_once()` behind the `EmailSender` port, run in-process (B1) for the first release, and move to B2 later without changing tables or the port. Wrong-decision cost is small.

#### Option C: in-process fire-and-forget after commit
How it works: after commit, the handler enqueues the send onto an in-memory queue or spawns a thread, and returns immediately.
- Pros: handler fast, no table, no polling loop.
- Cons: the queue is lost on crash, deploy or restart, and nothing records that an email was owed, so there is no way to detect or repair a miss; no durable retry; violates AC-3 "every"; harder to observe. The gap between commit and enqueue is itself a loss window.
- Verdict: rejected. Cheaper than B only until the first deploy mid-send.

#### Comparison against criteria
| Criterion | A sync | B outbox | C fire-and-forget |
|---|---|---|---|
| AC-3 every change emailed | no (lossy or duplicate-prone) | yes (durable, retried) | no (lossy) |
| NFR1 p95 < 300 ms | at risk (provider in path) | protected | protected |
| Failure isolation from provider (G2) | none | full | partial |
| Operability (visibility of backlog) | none | outbox depth/age, dead letters | none |
| New infra | none | drain loop, one table | thread/queue |

Recommendation: Option B with B1 first. Consistent with the scope notes' preliminary pick.

#### Design details the draft should carry for B (so the LLD owners get a precise input; not LLD redesign)
- Trigger rule: write an outbox row only when the event actually changes `orders.current_status` (the projection moves). A duplicate or older out-of-order event (ignored per d2) creates no email; this is the reading of "every status change" I assume (A-8). History-only late events do not notify.
- Content: email carries order reference, new status, timestamp, link to the order status page; no secrets, minimal PII (recipient resolved at send time from the order, stored by reference not copied into the outbox, to avoid a second PII copy; the port receives the address only for the call).
- Rendering: template per status chosen at send time from the status enum (A-4).
- Failure policy: retry with exponential backoff and jitter (proposal: 1 min doubling, cap about 1 h, max about 8 attempts, then `dead` plus an alert); permanent 4xx (bad address) goes to `dead` without further retries; 429/5xx/timeouts retry.
- Ordering: emails for one order should be sent in event order; drain by `created_at` per order and do not send event N+1 before N is terminal, or accept occasional reorder (A-9, minor; recommend simple per-order ordering because stale-looking emails confuse shoppers).
- Metrics: outbox pending count, oldest pending age, sends ok/failed/dead, send latency; alert on oldest pending age above a threshold (proposal 5 min) and any `dead` row.
- Retention: purge `sent` rows after a retention window (proposal 30 days) to bound table size.
- Test seams (NFR2 >= 90%): `EmailSender` port with a fake; `drain_once(now)` takes a clock, so backoff and dead-letter paths are unit-testable without sleeping.
- Feature flag: sending can be gated by `order_tracking_enabled` (scope Risks), while outbox rows are still written, so enabling later flushes nothing stale: add a rule that rows older than a cutoff are dropped, not sent, on first enable (open point, see Open questions).

Single-option check: three real alternatives exist, A and C are rejected on stated criteria, so this is not a single-option decision.

## Open questions

None blocks the design (user cannot answer; all recorded as assumptions for the draft):
- A-6 Carrier webhook retry behaviour (retry on non-2xx or timeout) is assumed standard; confirm in carrier docs at S3. It only strengthens the case against Option A.
- A-7 Whether the chosen email provider (undecided, C-3) honours an idempotency key. Design assumes at-least-once with a provider key where supported; a rare duplicate email is accepted otherwise. Confirm when the provider is picked; the port isolates this.
- A-8 "Every status change" means every change of the shopper-visible current status; duplicates and stale out-of-order events do not email. Options: (1) email only on projection change (recommended), (2) email on every accepted new event including stale ones. Team can overrule at review; ledger entry: none (assumption).
- A-9 Per-order email ordering: strict (recommended) vs best-effort. Team can settle at review.
- A-10 Backlog policy when the feature flag is first enabled: send or drop rows older than a cutoff. Recommend drop older than the cutoff (proposal 15 min) so shoppers do not get a burst of stale mail.
- A-11 Run the drain in-process (B1) first vs separate worker (B2): depends on deployment, which has no HLD view (no hld/deployment.md per scope notes). Recommend B1 with B2 as follow-up.
- Dependency: recipient address source. The shopper email and the order do not exist in code; they come from checkout/accounts (scope A-3, A-5, gap G-3). The outbox stores a reference, so this is a data dependency for S4, not a design blocker.

## Risks

- Drain loop is the first background process in the repo and deployment is undocumented. Wrong-choice cost is low: table and `EmailSender` port are independent of how the loop is hosted (B1 vs B2).
- Duplicate emails on crash between provider accept and `mark sent` (at-least-once). Mitigation: provider idempotency key = event_id where supported; unique(event_id) in the outbox; accept the rare duplicate as lesser than a lost email (AC-3 favors no loss).
- Multi-replica double-claim of the same row. Mitigation: atomic claim (row lock with skip-locked, or a `claimed_until` lease) in the drain query; test with two concurrent drains. DB choice is open (A-1), so the exact mechanism is decided in the data design.
- Outbox growth or stuck rows if the provider is down for long. Mitigation: bounded attempts and dead status, retention purge, alerts on oldest pending age and dead rows, manual requeue procedure in the runbook.
- Outbox write adds to the handler transaction: one extra insert, negligible against the 300 ms budget, but the load test in S5 must include it.
- Email latency: delivery latency is poll interval plus send time. Internal target below 1 min p95 (proposal); not an AC, not measured.
- PII: recipient address lives with the order, not copied to the outbox; error text stored in `last_error` must not echo addresses or provider tokens (scrub before storing).
- Provider outage visibility: with the outbox the failure is silent to the shopper unless alerts exist; S5 observability must ship before the flag goes on.

content.content:
1	## Analysis
2	
3	<!-- slice: scope -->
4	- Ticket: EVAL-1 "Order tracking", epic, feature order-tracking; AC-1 status+history per order, AC-2 carrier changes reach shop within a minute, AC-3 email on every status change (requirements.md, "Ticket EVAL-1").
5	- Feature PRD R1 status+history, R2 email on every change, R3 carrier updates move status (docs/product/features/order-tracking/prd.md lines 13-15). Dependencies: "None" (line 23) - but see drift/gap G-3 below.
6	- Product PRD: NFR1 "p95 API latency under 300 ms" (docs/product/prd.md line 28); NFR2 coverage >= 90% (line 29); G2 99.9% availability (line 17); F3 supports G1 (line 23).
7	- Code reality (src/shop/__init__.py lines 1-9): only `PAGE_SIZE`, `health()`, `list_customers()` stub. No web framework, no persistence, no order model, no HTTP layer, no email or carrier code. pyproject.toml: name shop 2.4.0, no dependencies, pytest pythonpath src. tests/test_health.py is the only test. So the design is greenfield: the order entity does not exist in code; F2 checkout (P0, roadmap Q4) that creates orders is also not built (docs/product/roadmap.md: Q4 checkout, Q1 order tracking).
8	- Framework/stack choice is not documented anywhere (no hld/tech-stack.md). The design stays framework-agnostic at the module level (`src/shop/tracking/`) and flags the HTTP layer as an assumption (A-1).
9	- Settled clarifications (clarify.py list): C-1 weigh webhook vs polling, pick simplest meeting p95 < 300 ms; C-2 callbacks authenticated, shared secret per carrier; C-3 outbound transactional email API, provider undecided and not design-relevant; C-4 epic fans out later, plan child slices in rollout, create no tickets.
10	- Design record folder: docs/architecture/lld/order-tracking/EVAL-1/ (task context). No analysis exists.
11	
12	## Decisions & candidate options
13	
14	<!-- slice: scope -->
15	### d1 Carrier status ingestion: webhook push vs API polling (settled by C-1: simplest option meeting NFR1)
16	- Option A webhook push: each carrier POSTs a signed callback to `POST /carriers/{carrier}/webhooks`; handler verifies, persists, acks. Pros: latency is carrier-recording to us in seconds, meets AC-2 (< 1 min) with margin; no scheduler, no per-order state to poll, no carrier rate-limit exposure; handler work is one signature check + one DB write so p95 stays far under 300 ms (NFR1) if email is off the request path (d3). Cons: public inbound endpoint (needs auth, C-2), carrier retries/duplicates/out-of-order need idempotency, missed callbacks (our downtime) are not self-healing.
17	- Option B status API polling: a scheduled job polls each carrier for all open orders. Pros: no inbound surface, no signature handling, we control pace. Cons: AC-2 needs a poll interval well under 60 s (worst-case latency = interval + call time), so all open shipments polled every ~20-30 s per carrier: cost and rate-limit risk grow with open orders; needs scheduler/worker infra that does not exist (src has none); more moving parts.
18	- Option C (hybrid: webhook primary plus low-frequency reconciliation poll). Considered and rejected for the first release as not the simplest (C-1); recorded as a follow-up to cover missed callbacks. Mitigation instead: carriers' own webhook retries, plus idempotent handler (d2).
19	- Preliminary pick: A. Evidence: AC-2 (requirements.md), NFR1 (prd.md:28), no scheduler in src/.
20	
21	### d2 Status data model: append-only event history vs single mutable status column
22	- Option A: `order_status_event` append-only table (order_id, carrier, carrier_event_id UNIQUE per carrier, status, occurred_at, received_at) plus `orders.current_status` projection updated in the same transaction. Pros: AC-1 history is a plain query; idempotency by unique (carrier, carrier_event_id); out-of-order handled by comparing occurred_at before moving current_status; email outbox row (d3) written in same txn. Cons: two writes per update; projection must stay consistent (same txn).
23	- Option B: only `orders.status` column, overwritten. Pros: simplest write. Cons: no history, fails AC-1 and PRD R1; no dedupe key. Rejected as not meeting requirements; kept as the strawman-free boundary: history could be derived from audit logs but is not queryable by shopper. Note: single-option-ish; real alternative is Option C: derive current status as latest event on read (no projection). Pros: one write, no consistency issue. Cons: read does an ordered lookup per order (index on (order_id, occurred_at) makes it cheap; list pages need a lateral/latest join, riskier for NFR1 on list view). Preliminary pick: A, with C as the fallback if projection drift is a concern.
24	- Order table does not exist in code (src/shop/__init__.py) nor in HLD (hld only has c4-context); F2 checkout (docs/product/features/checkout-with-card-payments/prd.md R1-R2) will create orders. This design defines only the tracking tables and an FK to orders; see gap G-3.
25	
26	### d3 Email on every status change: synchronous in handler vs transactional outbox with async sender
27	- Option A synchronous call to the email API inside the webhook handler. Pros: simplest, no worker. Cons: couples carrier ack latency (and retries) to a third party; email API slowness breaks NFR1 p95 < 300 ms and could make carriers retry, producing duplicate events; email failure would need to fail or swallow the callback.
28	- Option B transactional outbox: handler inserts `email_outbox` row in the same transaction as the event; a small sender (in-process background loop or separate worker process) drains the outbox, calls the provider API with retry/backoff, marks sent; idempotency key = event id so a retry never double-sends. Pros: keeps handler fast (NFR1), at-least-once with dedupe satisfies AC-3, provider-agnostic (C-3: only an `EmailSender` port needed). Cons: needs a drain loop (a minimal worker is new infra).
29	- Option C: fire-and-forget in-process thread/queue after commit. Pros: no table. Cons: lost emails on crash, violates AC-3 "every". Rejected unless user prefers; not recommended.
30	- Preliminary pick: B. The drain loop is the only background piece; it is also the natural slot for a later reconciliation poll (d1 option C).
31	
32	### d4 Callback authentication (C-2: shared secret per carrier)
33	- Option A: HMAC-SHA256 signature over the raw body with per-carrier secret, header e.g. `X-Signature`, plus timestamp header with tolerance (replay window), constant-time compare. Pros: integrity + authenticity, secret never on the wire, replay-bounded. Cons: needs raw-body access before parsing; both carriers must support signed push (the brief states both do: "support signed webhook push").
34	- Option B: static shared token in a header compared in constant time. Pros: trivial. Cons: secret travels on every request, no integrity, replayable; weaker, though acceptable only over TLS.
35	- Preliminary pick: A (brief says carriers support "signed webhook push", so A is available at no extra cost). Secrets stored via environment/secret store per carrier, rotation by accepting current+previous secret during overlap. Exact header names/algorithm per carrier is assumption A-2 to confirm against carrier docs at implementation.
36	
37	<!-- slice: d1 -->
38	### d1 Carrier status ingestion: webhook push vs status API polling vs hybrid
39	Settled input: C-1 (weigh both, pick the simplest meeting PRD p95 < 300 ms) and C-2 (shared secret per carrier), from the run prompt in requirements.md "Prompt" section, items (1) and (2). Both carriers support signed webhook push and status API polling (same source).
40	
41	Evidence:
42	- AC-2: "Carrier status changes reach the shop within a minute of the carrier recording them" (requirements.md, Acceptance criteria).
43	- NFR1: "p95 API latency under 300 ms" (docs/product/prd.md line 28, as cited in authoring-scope.md Analysis); G2 99.9% availability (prd.md line 17).
44	- Repo: `git ls-files` lists only src/shop/__init__.py and tests/test_health.py under code. Per authoring-scope.md Analysis, src has only `PAGE_SIZE`, `health()`, `list_customers()`; pyproject.toml has no dependencies. So there is no scheduler, worker, HTTP framework, persistence or carrier client. Any option adds its runtime from nothing; the question is which adds less.
45	
46	#### Option A: webhook push (preliminary winner)
47	How it works: each carrier POSTs a signed callback to one receiver route (proposed `POST /carriers/{carrier}/webhooks`). The handler reads the raw body, verifies the per-carrier HMAC and timestamp (d4, C-2), normalises the payload through a carrier adapter, writes the event and projection in one transaction (d2) and acks 2xx.
48	- AC-2: end-to-end latency is carrier send time plus our handler, typically seconds. Margin against 60 s is large. Carrier retry policy affects only failure cases (assumption A-D1-1 below).
49	- NFR1: handler does one HMAC check and one DB transaction, with no outbound calls (email is off-path per d3). This is bounded work, so p95 < 300 ms is plausible. Needs a load test (S5 in scope rollout).
50	- Simplicity: no scheduler, no per-order polling state, no carrier rate-limit management, no carrier credentials for outbound calls. Only a route and a verifier.
51	- Availability: carriers retry while we are down for short outages. Long outages leave status stale; no self-healing (see Option C).
52	- Security: public inbound endpoint. Needs raw-body HMAC, replay window, constant-time compare, body-size cap, rate limit.
53	- Cons: duplicates and out-of-order delivery need idempotency (unique carrier + carrier_event_id, occurred_at comparison, d2).
54	
55	#### Option B: status API polling
56	How it works: a scheduled job iterates open shipments per carrier, calls the carrier status API, diffs against the stored status and records changes.
57	- AC-2: worst-case latency is roughly poll interval + call duration + processing. To keep a safety margin under 60 s the interval must be about 30 s or less. Each open shipment is then polled about twice a minute per carrier, unless a carrier offers a bulk or since-cursor endpoint (unverified, assumption A-D1-2). Call volume grows linearly with open orders; rate limits and per-call costs are unknown.
58	- NFR1: the poller is not on a user-facing request path, so p95 of shopper endpoints is not directly affected. It does compete for DB and CPU with them.
59	- Simplicity: no inbound surface and no signature handling, but needs a scheduler/worker process, outbound carrier credentials, rate-limit and backoff logic and per-carrier clients. None of this exists in src.
60	- Availability: self-healing after our downtime (next poll catches up). But a carrier API outage stalls ingestion, and a long poll cycle can itself breach AC-2.

65	- Pros: closes the missed-callback gap and the long-outage availability concern against G2.
66	- Cons: needs everything Option B needs (scheduler, outbound clients, credentials) in addition to Option A, so it is strictly more than the simplest option. Fails C-1 "simplest" for the first release.
67	- Disposition: rejected for release 1, recorded as optional follow-up slice S6. It can share the outbox drain loop slot from d3 as the first background process, so adding it later is additive and does not change the handler or data model (event dedupe key makes polled and pushed events converge).

70	Option A. It is the simplest option that meets AC-2 with margin and NFR1 (C-1), requires no new scheduling infrastructure and authenticates with a per-carrier shared secret as C-2 allows. Option C stays as a documented, additive follow-up; the main residual risk (missed callbacks) is mitigated by carrier retries, an idempotent handler, and a stale-open-shipment alert.

80	### d2 Status data model (research slice; refines scope notes d2, authoring-scope.md lines 19-22)
81	
82	Drivers: AC-1 (current status AND history per order, requirements.md "Acceptance criteria"); idempotency and out-of-order carrier callbacks (d1 picks webhook push, so carriers retry and reorder; authoring-scope.md line 14); NFR1 p95 < 300 ms (docs/product/prd.md:28, as cited in scope notes line 5); AC-3 needs one email per status change, with an outbox row written in the same transaction (d3, scope line 26). Code evidence: src/shop/__init__.py (lines 1-9 per scope notes) has no persistence and no order model, so every option is greenfield and the orders table is owned by checkout (F2); the design only adds a FK to it (assumption A-5, scope line 90).
83	
84	#### Option A: append-only event table + orders.current_status projection, same transaction (recommended)
85	- How it works: `order_status_event(id, order_id FK, carrier, carrier_event_id, status, occurred_at, received_at, raw_payload_ref)`, UNIQUE(carrier, carrier_event_id), INDEX(order_id, occurred_at). `orders` gains `current_status` and `current_status_at`. Handler, in one transaction: INSERT event ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING; if 0 rows inserted it is a duplicate, so commit and ack 200 with no further effect (no second email). Otherwise UPDATE orders SET current_status, current_status_at WHERE id = ? AND (current_status_at IS NULL OR current_status_at < :occurred_at) (tie-break on event id); and INSERT email_outbox keyed by event id. The email decision is made on the status change event, not on projection movement (see Open questions Q1).
86	- Idempotency: DB-enforced via the unique key, so concurrent duplicate deliveries are safe without locks.
87	- Out-of-order: late event is still stored (history complete, AC-1) but cannot regress the projection, since the guarded UPDATE is conditional on occurred_at. History reads order by occurred_at, not received_at.
88	- AC-1: history = `SELECT ... WHERE order_id=? ORDER BY occurred_at`; current status = single column read. Order list page reads orders.current_status with no join, which protects NFR1 on list views.
89	- NFR1: write path is 1 INSERT + 1 conditional UPDATE + 1 outbox INSERT in one local transaction, no outbound calls: well under 300 ms.
90	- Cons: two sources of truth; projection can drift if any code path writes events without the projection. Mitigation: a single repository function is the only writer (module src/shop/tracking/), plus a consistency check query (current_status equals latest event) in tests and an ops job; projection is rebuildable from events at any time.
91	- Cost: storage grows by a few rows per order (6 normalised statuses, scope A-4); negligible.
92	
93	#### Option B: derive-on-read, events only (no projection)
94	- How it works: same event table and unique key; current status = latest event by occurred_at (`ORDER BY occurred_at DESC LIMIT 1`, or a lateral join for lists). No orders column.
95	- Pros: one write, no drift by construction, nothing to rebuild; idempotency and history identical to A.
96	- Cons: every order list needs a latest-per-order lookup; with the (order_id, occurred_at) index this is cheap for one order but a per-row lateral join on a page of orders is a larger NFR1 risk and couples checkout/order queries to the tracking table. The "did status change" decision for AC-3 needs a read of the previous latest event inside the transaction (a lock or serialisable read is needed to avoid two concurrent callbacks both deciding they changed it). Marginally weaker under concurrency than A's conditional UPDATE.
97	- Viability: genuinely viable at small scale; scale is not quantified in the PRD (assumption, see Risks).
98	
99	#### Option C: single mutable orders.status column, overwritten
100	- How it works: callback overwrites the column.
101	- Fails AC-1 (no history) and has no dedupe key, so duplicates cannot be told from changes (AC-3 would double-send), and an out-of-order callback regresses the status. Rejected as non-viable against requirements; listed for completeness, not a strawman for the choice between A and B.
102	
103	#### Option D (variant of A, noted): materialised view or cache of the latest event instead of a column
104	- Rejected: adds refresh lag against AC-2 and operational complexity for no gain over a column updated in-transaction.
105	
106	### Preliminary recommendation
107	Option A. It meets AC-1 with a trivial history query, gives DB-enforced idempotency, handles out-of-order without losing data, keeps list reads flat for NFR1, and the projection is always rebuildable from the log, which removes most of its drift risk. Fall back to Option B only if the team wants to avoid adding columns to the checkout-owned orders table (see Q2); the event table and handler contract are identical, so the switch is cheap.

110	### d3 Email on every status change (AC-3): synchronous vs transactional outbox vs fire-and-forget
111	
112	Evidence read: requirements.md (AC-3 "emailed on every order status change"; prompt answer 3: outbound transactional email API, provider undecided, does not change the design); authoring-scope.md d1-d3 and NFR checklist (NFR1 p95 < 300 ms from docs/product/prd.md:28 as cited there; G2 99.9%, prd.md:17); code reality per scope notes (src/shop/__init__.py lines 1-9: no framework, no persistence, no email, no background process; pyproject.toml has no dependencies). I did not re-open the PRD or src files in this slice; those citations are inherited from the scope notes.
113	
114	Constraints that frame the choice:
115	- AC-3 says "every" status change: a lost email is a requirement violation, so the delivery guarantee must be at-least-once with dedupe, not best-effort.
116	- NFR1 p95 < 300 ms applies to the webhook handler (d1 pick A) and the shopper endpoints. Handler is meant to be verify + one DB transaction (scope d1). A third-party call inside it puts provider latency into the p95.
117	- C-3: provider unknown, so the design needs a provider-agnostic `EmailSender` port.
118	- Carriers retry on non-2xx or timeout (assumption A-6 below). A handler that blocks on or fails because of the email API turns a mail outage into duplicate carrier callbacks.
119	- Operability: shop has no background process today and no deployment view (scope Architecture conformance call), so any new worker is new infra.
120	
121	#### Option A: synchronous send inside the webhook handler
122	How it works: after verifying and persisting the event, the handler calls `EmailSender.send()` and only then returns 2xx.
123	- Pros: fewest moving parts, no worker, no extra table; email is sent at once.
124	- Cons: provider latency adds directly to handler latency, so NFR1 p95 depends on a third party (typical transactional APIs are 100-500 ms per call, an assumption, not measured here, so one call alone can exceed the 300 ms budget). Provider failure forces a choice: fail the callback (carrier retries, duplicates, the event is already committed so dedupe must absorb it, and the email is still not guaranteed) or swallow the error (email lost, violating AC-3). Cannot retry with backoff without holding the carrier connection. Couples availability (G2) of ingestion to the email provider.
125	- Verdict: fails NFR1 risk and AC-3 reliability. Viable only as a prototype.
126	
127	#### Option B: transactional outbox with an async sender
128	How it works: in the same DB transaction that inserts the `order_status_event` and moves `orders.current_status`, the handler inserts one `email_outbox` row (columns proposed: id, event_id UNIQUE, order_id, recipient reference, status in pending/sent/failed/dead, attempts, next_attempt_at, created_at, sent_at, last_error). The handler returns 2xx after commit with no outbound call. A sender drains rows `WHERE status='pending' AND next_attempt_at <= now()` (claimed with row locking, e.g. `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, or an equivalent atomic claim, depending on the DB chosen, A-1), calls `EmailSender.send(idempotency_key=event_id)`, and marks sent; on error it increments attempts and sets `next_attempt_at` with exponential backoff, moving to `dead` after a cap (alerted).
129	- Pros: handler stays DB-only, protecting NFR1; the email intent is committed atomically with the status change, so no status change can exist without a pending email (AC-3 "every"); retries survive crashes and provider outages; unique(event_id) plus the provider idempotency key gives effectively-once sending; unique(event_id) also makes a duplicate carrier callback (already deduped on carrier_event_id in d2) unable to enqueue a second email; adds natural metrics (outbox depth, oldest pending age). The same drain loop can later host the reconciliation poll (scope d1 option C).
130	- Cons: new background component; one more table; delivery latency is the drain interval plus send time (poll interval proposal 1-5 s, or wake-on-insert signal, so email lands well within a minute; this is a proposed internal target, not a requirement); at-least-once means a crash between provider accept and `mark sent` can double-send unless the provider honours the idempotency key (assumption A-7), otherwise a rare duplicate email is accepted.
131	- Sub-choice B1, in-process drain loop (thread/async task started with the app): simplest deploy, no new process type; with several app replicas it needs the row-claim lock above, and a stuck app stops sending. Sub-choice B2, separate worker process: independent scaling and failure isolation, but needs a second deployable that deployment docs do not define yet. Recommendation: build the drain as a plain function `drain_once()` behind the `EmailSender` port, run in-process (B1) for the first release, and move to B2 later without changing tables or the port. Wrong-decision cost is small.
132	
133	#### Option C: in-process fire-and-forget after commit
134	How it works: after commit, the handler enqueues the send onto an in-memory queue or spawns a thread, and returns immediately.
135	- Pros: handler fast, no table, no polling loop.
136	- Cons: the queue is lost on crash, deploy or restart, and nothing records that an email was owed, so there is no way to detect or repair a miss; no durable retry; violates AC-3 "every"; harder to observe. The gap between commit and enqueue is itself a loss window.
137	- Verdict: rejected. Cheaper than B only until the first deploy mid-send.
138	
139	#### Comparison against criteria
140	| Criterion | A sync | B outbox | C fire-and-forget |
141	|---|---|---|---|
142	| AC-3 every change emailed | no (lossy or duplicate-prone) | yes (durable, retried) | no (lossy) |
143	| NFR1 p95 < 300 ms | at risk (provider in path) | protected | protected |
144	| Failure isolation from provider (G2) | none | full | partial |
145	| Operability (visibility of backlog) | none | outbox depth/age, dead letters | none |
146	| New infra | none | drain loop, one table | thread/queue |
147	
148	Recommendation: Option B with B1 first. Consistent with the scope notes' preliminary pick.
149	
150	#### Design details the draft should carry for B (so the LLD owners get a precise input; not LLD redesign)
151	- Trigger rule: write an outbox row only when the event actually changes `orders.current_status` (the projection moves). A duplicate or older out-of-order event (ignored per d2) creates no email; this is the reading of "every status change" I assume (A-8). History-only late events do not notify.
152	- Content: email carries order reference, new status, timestamp, link to the order status page; no secrets, minimal PII (recipient resolved at send time from the order, stored by reference not copied into the outbox, to avoid a second PII copy; the port receives the address only for the call).
153	- Rendering: template per status chosen at send time from the status enum (A-4).
154	- Failure policy: retry with exponential backoff and jitter (proposal: 1 min doubling, cap about 1 h, max about 8 attempts, then `dead` plus an alert); permanent 4xx (bad address) goes to `dead` without further retries; 429/5xx/timeouts retry.
155	- Ordering: emails for one order should be sent in event order; drain by `created_at` per order and do not send event N+1 before N is terminal, or accept occasional reorder (A-9, minor; recommend simple per-order ordering because stale-looking emails confuse shoppers).
156	- Metrics: outbox pending count, oldest pending age, sends ok/failed/dead, send latency; alert on oldest pending age above a threshold (proposal 5 min) and any `dead` row.
157	- Retention: purge `sent` rows after a retention window (proposal 30 days) to bound table size.
158	- Test seams (NFR2 >= 90%): `EmailSender` port with a fake; `drain_once(now)` takes a clock, so backoff and dead-letter paths are unit-testable without sleeping.
159	- Feature flag: sending can be gated by `order_tracking_enabled` (scope Risks), while outbox rows are still written, so enabling later flushes nothing stale: add a rule that rows older than a cutoff are dropped, not sent, on first enable (open point, see Open questions).
160	
161	Single-option check: three real alternatives exist, A and C are rejected on stated criteria, so this is not a single-option decision.

164	### d4 Callback authentication for carrier webhooks (settled input: C-2 callbacks authenticated, shared secret per carrier acceptable; requirements.md Prompt item 2)
165	
166	Evidence read: requirements.md (Prompt items 1-2: both carriers "support signed webhook push"; AC-2 within a minute); authoring-scope.md (## Decisions d4 lines 30-33, NFR checklist Security line 37, d2 unique (carrier, carrier_event_id) line 20, Risks "Secret leakage/rotation" line 97, A-2 line 90). Code reality from scope notes: src/shop/__init__.py lines 1-9 is a stub and pyproject.toml has no dependencies, so any option should use the Python standard library only (`hmac`, `hashlib`, `secrets`); I did not re-open src in this slice.
167	
168	Shared facts for both options:
169	- Endpoint is `POST /carriers/{carrier}/webhooks` (scope d1 option A). The `{carrier}` path segment selects which secret to use; an unknown carrier gets 404 with no secret lookup.
170	- Failure response is a uniform 401 that does not reveal which check failed (scope NFR Security line 37). Verification runs BEFORE any parsing or DB write, so an unauthenticated caller costs one HMAC/compare, and the NFR1 p95 < 300 ms budget (prd.md:28 per scope line 5) is not at risk.
171	- Replay: d2 already makes the handler idempotent via unique (carrier, carrier_event_id), so a replayed valid body creates no second event and no second email (d3 outbox row is written in the same transaction). The auth layer therefore only needs to bound replay, not eliminate it.
172	
173	#### Option A: HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body plus timestamp (recommended)
174	How it works: carrier sends `X-Signature` (hex or base64 HMAC-SHA256) and `X-Timestamp`. Shop computes HMAC over `timestamp + "." + raw_body` with the carrier's secret, compares with `hmac.compare_digest`, and rejects when |now - timestamp| exceeds a tolerance (proposed 5 minutes, configurable). Raw bytes must be captured before JSON parsing. Rotation: each carrier has an ordered list of at most two secrets (current, previous); verification tries both, so the carrier can switch on its own schedule; remove the previous secret after the overlap window.
175	Pros: secret never on the wire; body integrity (tampering of status, order or tracking number is detected); replay bounded by the timestamp window and made harmless by d2 dedupe; matches the brief that both carriers "support signed webhook push", so no carrier-side extra work; stdlib only, so no new dependency; rotation without downtime.
176	Cons: raw-body access is needed (framework choice is undecided, A-1; must be a requirement on the HTTP layer); depends on carrier signature scheme (exact header names, encoding, whether timestamp is signed; A-2); clock skew between carrier and shop can cause false rejects (mitigated by tolerance and NTP); a carrier that re-sends retries with the ORIGINAL timestamp could be rejected after the window, losing events (see Risks).
177	Implementation cost: low-moderate; one pure function `verify_signature(secret_list, headers, raw_body, now)` per carrier adapter, trivially unit-testable (supports NFR2 >= 90%, scope line 40).
178	
179	#### Option B: static shared token in a header, constant-time compare
180	How it works: carrier sends `Authorization: Bearer <token>` or `X-Carrier-Token`; shop compares against the per-carrier token with `hmac.compare_digest` over TLS. Rotation: accept current+previous token.
181	Pros: simplest to build and to configure on the carrier side; no raw-body capture, no clock dependency; works even if a carrier's signing is awkward.
182	Cons: the secret is sent on every request, so any TLS-terminating proxy, access log or APM tool that captures headers leaks it (scope Security line 37 already forbids logging secrets, which is harder to enforce for headers); no integrity (a valid token authorises any body); fully replayable by anyone who observes one request, so replay is limited only by d2 dedupe, and a captured token allows forging NEW events with fresh event ids; does not use the signed push capability the carriers already offer.
183	Implementation cost: lowest, but the saving over A is small (about one function), so it does not buy much.
184	
185	#### Option C (considered, not a standalone choice): network controls only (mTLS or carrier IP allowlist)
186	Stronger transport identity if both carriers offer mTLS or fixed egress IPs, but this is unconfirmed (no source says so), adds certificate or ingress operations that do not exist (no hld/deployment.md per scope line 45), and does not satisfy C-2's "shared secret per carrier" framing. Recorded as an optional defence-in-depth layer at the edge, not as the application-level decision.
187	
188	#### Comparison against criteria
189	| Criterion | A: HMAC + timestamp | B: static token |
190	|---|---|---|
191	| Security (C-2, NFR) | Authenticity + integrity, secret not sent | Authenticity only, secret sent each call |
192	| Replay | Bounded by window, harmless via d2 | Unbounded, only d2 dedupe |
193	| Rotation | Current+previous secret overlap | Current+previous token overlap |
194	| Compromise via logs/proxy | Signature is single-use-ish, secret not exposed | Token exposed, forgery possible |
195	| Implementation cost | Low-moderate, stdlib | Lowest, stdlib |
196	| Dependency on carrier | Needs signed push (stated available) | Needs custom header support (assumed) |
197	| Perf impact (NFR1) | One HMAC over small body, negligible | Negligible |
198	
199	#### Recommendation for d4
200	Option A. B loses on the security NFR for a marginal saving, and the carriers' signed push is stated as available (requirements.md Prompt item 1). Concrete parameters to put in the draft: per-carrier secret list in env/secret store (never in repo or logs), constant-time compare, 5-minute tolerance (proposal, tunable), uniform 401, 64 KiB body cap checked before hashing (proposal), metrics `callbacks_rejected{reason}` with the reason kept in metrics/internal logs only, not in the response. Fall back to B only for a carrier that proves unable to sign, as a per-carrier adapter setting, and then require TLS plus the edge controls from Option C; that fallback is itself a risk acceptance for the team to note at review.
201	
202	Assumptions (flagged, user cannot answer; confirm in the carrier adapter slice S3):
203	- A-2 (carried from scope): exact header names, digest encoding, signed string layout and timestamp semantics per carrier come from carrier docs, not from anything in the repo.
204	- A-d4-1: carriers re-sign each retry with a fresh timestamp. If a carrier retries with the original timestamp, set the tolerance above its maximum retry horizon, because d2 idempotency makes a wide window safe.
205	- A-d4-2: each carrier can hold two secrets or can switch at an agreed time, so overlap-based rotation works; if not, rotation needs a short agreed maintenance window.
206	- A-d4-3: the HTTP layer (undecided, A-1) can expose the unparsed request body.

# Tech design — EVAL-1: Order tracking

## Decision & options

Decision: receive carrier status changes by signed webhook push (HMAC-SHA256 per carrier secret), store them as an append-only event history with an in-transaction `orders.current_status` projection, and send shopper emails from a transactional outbox drained off the request path behind a provider-agnostic `EmailSender` port.

### Context

- Problem: shoppers must track an order from payment to delivery: status and history (AC-1), carrier changes reaching the shop within a minute (AC-2), and an email on every status change (AC-3). Feature PRD R1-R3 (`docs/product/features/order-tracking/prd.md` lines 13-15), product feature F3, supports G1.
- Scope: epic-level design. Child slices are laid out in Rollout & migration, and no child tickets are created now (C-4).
- Binding constraints: NFR1 p95 API latency under 300 ms and NFR2 coverage at least 90% (`docs/product/prd.md` NFR section), G2 99.9% availability.
- Codebase reality: `src/shop/__init__.py` has only `PAGE_SIZE`, `health()` and `list_customers()`. `pyproject.toml` lists no dependencies. There is no HTTP framework, persistence, order model, scheduler, email or carrier code. The design is greenfield and names modules (`src/shop/tracking/`) and contracts, not libraries (A-1).
- Settled decisions (clarification ledger):
  - C-1: weigh webhook against polling and pick the simplest option that meets p95 < 300 ms.
  - C-2: carrier callbacks are authenticated, and a shared secret per carrier is acceptable.
  - C-3: email goes through an outbound transactional email API. The provider is undecided and does not change the design.
  - C-4: the epic is fanned out later, so child slices are planned in the rollout and no tickets are created.
- Assumptions: A-1 to A-5 are listed under Open questions.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  carrier["Carrier A / B"] -->|"signed webhook"| rx["Webhook receiver"]
  rx -->|"one transaction"| db[("order_status_event, orders.current_status, email_outbox")]
  db --> drain["Outbox drain (EmailSender port)"]
  drain --> mail["Transactional email API"]
  shopper["Shopper"] -->|"status and history"| api["Shopper read API"]
  api --> db
```

### Options considered

#### Decision d1: carrier status ingestion

##### Option A: webhook push (chosen)
Each carrier POSTs a signed callback to one receiver route. The handler verifies, normalises through a carrier adapter, writes in one transaction and acks.
- Pros: latency is seconds, so AC-2 has a large margin. There is no scheduler, polling state or rate-limit exposure. The handler is one signature check plus one transaction with no outbound calls, so p95 < 300 ms is plausible (to be proven by the S5 load test).
- Cons: public inbound surface, needs idempotency for duplicate and reordered deliveries, and missed callbacks during our downtime are not self-healing.

##### Option B: status API polling
A scheduled job polls each carrier for all open shipments.
- AC-2 forces an interval of about 30 s or less (worst case is interval plus call time), so each open shipment is polled about twice a minute per carrier. Cost and rate-limit risk grow with open orders (bulk endpoints are unverified, A-D1-2).
- Needs a scheduler or worker, outbound credentials and per-carrier clients, none of which exist. It self-heals after downtime but a carrier API outage stalls ingestion.

##### Option C: hybrid (webhook plus slow reconciliation poll)
Closes the missed-callback gap but needs everything Option B needs on top of Option A, so it is not the simplest (C-1). It is rejected for release 1 and kept as the additive follow-up S6.

#### Decision d2: status data model

##### Option A: append-only `order_status_event` plus `orders.current_status` projection in the same transaction (chosen)
- Mechanics:
  - The table is UNIQUE(carrier, carrier_event_id) with INDEX(order_id, occurred_at).
  - The handler runs INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. A conflict means a duplicate, so it acks with no further effect.
  - Otherwise it runs an UPDATE of `orders` guarded by `current_status_at < occurred_at`, plus an `email_outbox` insert only when the projection moved.
- Pros:
  - History is a plain ordered query (AC-1).
  - Idempotency is enforced by the database without locks.
  - A late event is stored but cannot regress the projection.
  - List pages read one column with no join, which protects NFR1.
  - The projection is rebuildable from events.
- Cons: two sources of truth. Mitigation: a single writer function, an invariant test and a rebuild script.

##### Option B: events only, derive the current status on read
- Pros: one write and no drift.
- Cons: lists need a latest-per-order lateral join (an NFR1 risk), and the "did status change" decision for AC-3 needs a lock or serialisable read. It is viable at small scale and is the fallback if the team does not want columns added to the checkout-owned `orders` table. The event table and handler contract are identical, so switching is cheap.

##### Option C: single mutable `orders.status` column
Fails AC-1 (no history), has no dedupe key and regresses on out-of-order callbacks. It is not viable against the requirements and is listed for completeness only.

#### Decision d3: email on every status change

##### Option A: synchronous send inside the webhook handler
- Pros: simplest, with no worker.
- Cons: provider latency lands in the handler p95 (NFR1 at risk) and couples ingestion availability (G2) to the provider. Failing the callback causes carrier retries and duplicates, and swallowing the error loses the email (violates AC-3). Rejected.

##### Option B: transactional outbox with an async sender (chosen)
- The handler inserts an `email_outbox` row (unique `event_id`) in the same transaction and returns. A `drain_once(now)` function claims pending rows atomically, calls `EmailSender.send(idempotency_key=event_id)` and retries with exponential backoff, moving to `dead` after a cap.
- Pros:
  - No status change can exist without a pending email.
  - The handler stays DB-only.
  - Retries survive crashes and provider outages.
  - Backlog age and depth are observable.
  - The provider stays behind the port (C-3).
- Cons: a new background component and one more table. A crash between provider accept and `mark sent` can double-send unless the provider honours the idempotency key (A-7).
- Hosting sub-choice: in-process drain loop first (B1), separate worker later (B2). Tables and the port do not change between them.

##### Option C: in-process fire-and-forget after commit
Nothing records that an email was owed, so a crash or deploy loses mail, which violates "every". Rejected.

#### Decision d4: callback authentication (C-2)

##### Option A: HMAC-SHA256 over timestamp plus raw body, per-carrier secret (chosen)
- Mechanics:
  - Compare with `hmac.compare_digest`.
  - Tolerance of 5 minutes (proposal, configurable).
  - Rotation by accepting a current and a previous secret.
  - Verification runs before parsing or any DB write.
  - Uniform 401 with no detail.
  - Body cap of 64 KiB (proposal).
- Pros:
  - The secret never travels on the wire.
  - Body integrity.
  - Replay is bounded by the window and made harmless by the d2 unique key.
  - Standard library only.
  - Both carriers support signed push.
- Cons: needs raw-body access from the HTTP layer (A-1), depends on carrier scheme details (A-2), and clock skew or retries carrying the original timestamp can cause false rejects.

##### Option B: static shared token in a header
- Pros: simplest, with no raw-body or clock dependency.
- Cons: the secret is sent on every request and can leak via proxy or access logs, there is no integrity, and a captured token allows forging new events. The saving over A is about one function.
- Kept only as a per-carrier fallback if a carrier cannot sign. That needs explicit team risk acceptance.

##### Option C: network controls only (mTLS or IP allowlist)
Unconfirmed carrier support, no deployment view, and it does not match C-2. Recorded as optional edge defence-in-depth.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Carrier
  participant R as Webhook receiver
  participant D as Database
  participant S as Outbox drain
  participant M as Email API
  C->>R: POST /carriers/{carrier}/webhooks (signed)
  R->>R: verify HMAC and timestamp, then normalise
  R->>D: one transaction: event, projection, outbox row
  R-->>C: 2xx
  S->>D: claim pending outbox rows
  S->>M: send (idempotency key = event id)
  S->>D: mark sent or schedule retry
```

### Rationale

- d1: webhook push is the simplest option meeting AC-2 with margin and NFR1 (C-1). Polling adds a scheduler, outbound credentials and per-shipment cost to hit a one-minute target. The hybrid is strictly more, so it is deferred as S6.
- d2: the event log with a projection gives AC-1 history, database-enforced idempotency and flat list reads. Derive-on-read is the cheap fallback.
- d3: AC-3 says "every", so durable at-least-once delivery with dedupe is required. The outbox also protects the NFR1 handler budget and decouples ingestion from the provider (C-3).
- d4: C-2 allows a shared secret, and HMAC is that secret used safely. The brief says both carriers already support signed push, so the extra security costs almost nothing.
- Email trigger rule: an email is sent only when `current_status` actually changes. Duplicates and stale out-of-order events are stored in history but do not email (A-8).

- ADR: Order status history as append-only events with an in-transaction current-status projection.
- ADR: Shopper emails through a transactional outbox and an `EmailSender` port, with the provider left open (C-3).
- ADR: Authenticate carrier callbacks with per-carrier HMAC-SHA256 and a timestamp window (C-2).
