1	---
2	status: "proposed"
3	version: 1
4	tickets:
5	  - "EVAL-1"
6	feature: "order-tracking"
7	---
8	
9	# Tech design — EVAL-1: Order tracking
10	
11	## Decision & options
12	
13	Decision: receive carrier status changes by signed webhook push (HMAC-SHA256 per carrier secret), store them as an append-only event history with an in-transaction `orders.current_status` projection, and send shopper emails from a transactional outbox drained off the request path behind a provider-agnostic `EmailSender` port.
14	
15	### Context
16	
17	- Problem: shoppers must track an order from payment to delivery: status and history (AC-1), carrier changes reaching the shop within a minute (AC-2), and an email on every status change (AC-3). Feature PRD R1-R3 (`docs/product/features/order-tracking/prd.md` lines 13-15), product feature F3, supports G1.
18	- Scope: epic-level design. Child slices are laid out in Rollout & migration, and no child tickets are created now (C-4).
19	- Binding constraints: NFR1 p95 API latency under 300 ms and NFR2 coverage at least 90% (`docs/product/prd.md` NFR section), G2 99.9% availability.
20	- Codebase reality: `src/shop/__init__.py` has only `PAGE_SIZE`, `health()` and `list_customers()`. `pyproject.toml` lists no dependencies. There is no HTTP framework, persistence, order model, scheduler, email or carrier code. The design is greenfield and names modules (`src/shop/tracking/`) and contracts, not libraries (A-1).
21	- Settled decisions (clarification ledger):
22	  - C-1: weigh webhook against polling and pick the simplest option that meets p95 < 300 ms.
23	  - C-2: carrier callbacks are authenticated, and a shared secret per carrier is acceptable.
24	  - C-3: email goes through an outbound transactional email API. The provider is undecided and does not change the design.
25	  - C-4: the epic is fanned out later, so child slices are planned in the rollout and no tickets are created.
26	- Assumptions: A-1 to A-5 are listed under Open questions.
27	
28	```mermaid
29	flowchart LR
30	  carrier["Carrier A / B"] -->|"signed webhook"| rx["Webhook receiver"]
31	  rx -->|"one transaction"| db[("order_status_event, orders.current_status, email_outbox")]
32	  db --> drain["Outbox drain (EmailSender port)"]
33	  drain --> mail["Transactional email API"]
34	  shopper["Shopper"] -->|"status and history"| api["Shopper read API"]
35	  api --> db
36	```
37	
38	### Options considered
39	
40	#### Decision d1: carrier status ingestion
41	
42	##### Option A: webhook push (chosen)
43	Each carrier POSTs a signed callback to one receiver route. The handler verifies, normalises through a carrier adapter, writes in one transaction and acks.
44	- Pros: latency is seconds, so AC-2 has a large margin. There is no scheduler, polling state or rate-limit exposure. The handler is one signature check plus one transaction with no outbound calls, so p95 < 300 ms is plausible (to be proven by the S5 load test).
45	- Cons: public inbound surface, needs idempotency for duplicate and reordered deliveries, and missed callbacks during our downtime are not self-healing.
46	
47	##### Option B: status API polling
48	A scheduled job polls each carrier for all open shipments.
49	- AC-2 forces an interval of about 30 s or less (worst case is interval plus call time), so each open shipment is polled about twice a minute per carrier. Cost and rate-limit risk grow with open orders (bulk endpoints are unverified, A-D1-2).
50	- Needs a scheduler or worker, outbound credentials and per-carrier clients, none of which exist. It self-heals after downtime but a carrier API outage stalls ingestion.
51	
52	##### Option C: hybrid (webhook plus slow reconciliation poll)
53	Closes the missed-callback gap but needs everything Option B needs on top of Option A, so it is not the simplest (C-1). It is rejected for release 1 and kept as the additive follow-up S6.
54	
55	#### Decision d2: status data model
56	
57	##### Option A: append-only `order_status_event` plus `orders.current_status` projection in the same transaction (chosen)
58	- Mechanics:
59	  - The table is UNIQUE(carrier, carrier_event_id) with INDEX(order_id, occurred_at).
60	  - The handler runs INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. A conflict means a duplicate, so it acks with no further effect.
61	  - Otherwise it runs an UPDATE of `orders` guarded by `current_status_at < occurred_at`, plus an `email_outbox` insert only when the projection moved.
62	- Pros:
63	  - History is a plain ordered query (AC-1).
64	  - Idempotency is enforced by the database without locks.
65	  - A late event is stored but cannot regress the projection.
66	  - List pages read one column with no join, which protects NFR1.
67	  - The projection is rebuildable from events.
68	- Cons: two sources of truth. Mitigation: a single writer function, an invariant test and a rebuild script.
69	
70	##### Option B: events only, derive the current status on read
71	- Pros: one write and no drift.
72	- Cons: lists need a latest-per-order lateral join (an NFR1 risk), and the "did status change" decision for AC-3 needs a lock or serialisable read. It is viable at small scale and is the fallback if the team does not want columns added to the checkout-owned `orders` table. The event table and handler contract are identical, so switching is cheap.
73	
74	##### Option C: single mutable `orders.status` column
75	Fails AC-1 (no history), has no dedupe key and regresses on out-of-order callbacks. It is not viable against the requirements and is listed for completeness only.
76	
77	#### Decision d3: email on every status change
78	
79	##### Option A: synchronous send inside the webhook handler
80	- Pros: simplest, with no worker.
81	- Cons: provider latency lands in the handler p95 (NFR1 at risk) and couples ingestion availability (G2) to the provider. Failing the callback causes carrier retries and duplicates, and swallowing the error loses the email (violates AC-3). Rejected.
82	
83	##### Option B: transactional outbox with an async sender (chosen)
84	- The handler inserts an `email_outbox` row (unique `event_id`) in the same transaction and returns. A `drain_once(now)` function claims pending rows atomically, calls `EmailSender.send(idempotency_key=event_id)` and retries with exponential backoff, moving to `dead` after a cap.
85	- Pros:
86	  - No status change can exist without a pending email.
87	  - The handler stays DB-only.
88	  - Retries survive crashes and provider outages.
89	  - Backlog age and depth are observable.
90	  - The provider stays behind the port (C-3).
91	- Cons: a new background component and one more table. A crash between provider accept and `mark sent` can double-send unless the provider honours the idempotency key (A-7).
92	- Hosting sub-choice: in-process drain loop first (B1), separate worker later (B2). Tables and the port do not change between them.
93	
94	##### Option C: in-process fire-and-forget after commit
95	Nothing records that an email was owed, so a crash or deploy loses mail, which violates "every". Rejected.
96	
97	#### Decision d4: callback authentication (C-2)
98	
99	##### Option A: HMAC-SHA256 over timestamp plus raw body, per-carrier secret (chosen)
100	- Mechanics:
101	  - Compare with `hmac.compare_digest`.
102	  - Tolerance of 5 minutes (proposal, configurable).
103	  - Rotation by accepting a current and a previous secret.
104	  - Verification runs before parsing or any DB write.
105	  - Uniform 401 with no detail.
106	  - Body cap of 64 KiB (proposal).
107	- Pros:
108	  - The secret never travels on the wire.
109	  - Body integrity.
110	  - Replay is bounded by the window and made harmless by the d2 unique key.
111	  - Standard library only.
112	  - Both carriers support signed push.
113	- Cons: needs raw-body access from the HTTP layer (A-1), depends on carrier scheme details (A-2), and clock skew or retries carrying the original timestamp can cause false rejects.
114	
115	##### Option B: static shared token in a header
116	- Pros: simplest, with no raw-body or clock dependency.
117	- Cons: the secret is sent on every request and can leak via proxy or access logs, there is no integrity, and a captured token allows forging new events. The saving over A is about one function.
118	- Kept only as a per-carrier fallback if a carrier cannot sign. That needs explicit team risk acceptance.
119	
120	##### Option C: network controls only (mTLS or IP allowlist)
121	Unconfirmed carrier support, no deployment view, and it does not match C-2. Recorded as optional edge defence-in-depth.
122	
123	```mermaid
124	sequenceDiagram
125	  participant C as Carrier
126	  participant R as Webhook receiver
127	  participant D as Database
128	  participant S as Outbox drain
129	  participant M as Email API
130	  C->>R: POST /carriers/{carrier}/webhooks (signed)
131	  R->>R: verify HMAC and timestamp, then normalise
132	  R->>D: one transaction: event, projection, outbox row
133	  R-->>C: 2xx
134	  S->>D: claim pending outbox rows
135	  S->>M: send (idempotency key = event id)
136	  S->>D: mark sent or schedule retry
137	```

139	### Rationale
140	
141	- d1: webhook push is the simplest option meeting AC-2 with margin and NFR1 (C-1). Polling adds a scheduler, outbound credentials and per-shipment cost to hit a one-minute target. The hybrid is strictly more, so it is deferred as S6.
142	- d2: the event log with a projection gives AC-1 history, database-enforced idempotency and flat list reads. Derive-on-read is the cheap fallback.
143	- d3: AC-3 says "every", so durable at-least-once delivery with dedupe is required. The outbox also protects the NFR1 handler budget and decouples ingestion from the provider (C-3).
144	- d4: C-2 allows a shared secret, and HMAC is that secret used safely. The brief says both carriers already support signed push, so the extra security costs almost nothing.
145	- Email trigger rule: an email is sent only when `current_status` actually changes. Duplicates and stale out-of-order events are stored in history but do not email (A-8).

211	## NFRs
212	
213	- **Security (required)**
214	  - Callbacks are authenticated by HMAC over the raw body with a timestamp window and a constant-time compare. Verification runs first, with a uniform 401 and the reason kept in metrics only.
215	  - Secrets are held per carrier in the environment or a secret store, never in the repo or logs. Rotation accepts the current and previous secret.
216	  - The public endpoint has a 64 KiB body cap and edge rate limiting (S5), and is TLS only.
217	  - Shopper endpoints return only the caller's own orders. The shopper authentication mechanism is undefined (A-3).
218	  - PII: the recipient is resolved at send time and passed only to the email provider. The outbox stores a reference, and `last_error` is scrubbed. Raw payloads are stored minimised or by reference.
219	- **Performance (required)**
220	  - NFR1: webhook p95 < 300 ms. The handler budget is one HMAC, one transaction (insert, conditional update, outbox insert) and no outbound calls.
221	  - Shopper status and history endpoints are also held to p95 < 300 ms. They are served by the (order_id, occurred_at) index and a flat `current_status` column. The S5 load test proves both.
222	  - AC-2: push latency is seconds against a 60 s target.
223	  - Internal proposal, not a requirement: outbox delivery delay p95 under 1 minute, with a drain interval of 1-5 s.
224	- **Availability** (G2 99.9%): carrier retries cover short outages. Long outages are covered later by S6. Alert on open shipments with no event beyond a threshold.
225	- **Operability**: metrics for callbacks received, rejected and duplicate, outbox depth, oldest pending age, sends ok/failed/dead, and send latency. Alert on any `dead` row.
226	- **Reliability**: the handler and sender are idempotent, with exponential backoff and a max of about 8 attempts (proposal).
227	- **Cost**: no polling cost. One email per status change.
228	- **Compliance**: shopper email is personal data. The PRD is silent, so the design applies minimisation only.
229	- **Testability** (NFR2 at least 90%): the verifier, adapters and ordering logic are pure functions. The email port has a fake, and `drain_once` takes a clock.

231	## Risks
232	
233	- Blast radius: new module `src/shop/tracking/`, three data changes, and one new public endpoint. The `orders` table is owned by checkout (F2). No existing code changes, since `src` holds only stubs. Affected components are checkout (F2), order management (F4) and the platform shopper authentication.
234	- Orders dependency (highest): no orders entity or checkout exists (roadmap Q4 checkout precedes Q1 tracking). Mitigation: S1 ships a minimal stub if `orders` is not ready.
235	- Missed callbacks (downtime, or carrier retry policy unknown, A-D1-1). Mitigation: carrier retries, idempotent handler, stale-shipment alert and S6. If retries are absent, S6 becomes required.
236	- Wrong signature assumption (A-2) would reject all genuine callbacks. Mitigation: per-carrier verifier, contract tests with carrier sample payloads, and a staging run before the flag is enabled.
237	- Timestamp window or clock skew rejects genuine retries. Mitigation: wide tolerance (safe because of dedupe), NTP, and an alert on timestamp rejects.
238	- Projection drift. Mitigation: a single writer, an invariant test and a rebuild script. Events remain the truth.
239	- Duplicate emails after a crash. Mitigation: unique event_id plus the provider idempotency key (A-7). A rare duplicate is accepted over a lost email.
240	- Multi-replica double claim of an outbox row. Mitigation: an atomic claim and a two-drain concurrency test.
241	- First background process in the repo, with no deployment view. The wrong choice costs only a refactor of the drain loop hosting.
242	- NFR1 is not proven by design. S5 must include the outbox insert in its load test. Order and event volumes are not in the PRD (assumed modest).
243	- Fallback to a static token for an unable-to-sign carrier weakens security and needs explicit risk acceptance.

15	### d1 Carrier status ingestion: webhook push vs API polling (settled by C-1: simplest option meeting NFR1)
16	- Option A webhook push: each carrier POSTs a signed callback to `POST /carriers/{carrier}/webhooks`; handler verifies, persists, acks. Pros: latency is carrier-recording to us in seconds, meets AC-2 (< 1 min) with margin; no scheduler, no per-order state to poll, no carrier rate-limit exposure; handler work is one signature check + one DB write so p95 stays far under 300 ms (NFR1) if email is off the request path (d3). Cons: public inbound endpoint (needs auth, C-2), carrier retries/duplicates/out-of-order need idempotency, missed callbacks (our downtime) are not self-healing.
17	- Option B status API polling: a scheduled job polls each carrier for all open orders. Pros: no inbound surface, no signature handling, we control pace. Cons: AC-2 needs a poll interval well under 60 s (worst-case latency = interval + call time), so all open shipments polled every ~20-30 s per carrier: cost and rate-limit risk grow with open orders; needs scheduler/worker infra that does not exist (src has none); more moving parts.
18	- Option C (hybrid: webhook primary plus low-frequency reconciliation poll). Considered and rejected for the first release as not the simplest (C-1); recorded as a follow-up to cover missed callbacks. Mitigation instead: carriers' own webhook retries, plus idempotent handler (d2).
19	- Preliminary pick: A. Evidence: AC-2 (requirements.md), NFR1 (prd.md:28), no scheduler in src/.

38	### d1 Carrier status ingestion: webhook push vs status API polling vs hybrid
39	Settled input: C-1 (weigh both, pick the simplest meeting PRD p95 < 300 ms) and C-2 (shared secret per carrier), from the run prompt in requirements.md "Prompt" section, items (1) and (2). Both carriers support signed webhook push and status API polling (same source).
40	
41	Evidence:
42	- AC-2: "Carrier status changes reach the shop within a minute of the carrier recording them" (requirements.md, Acceptance criteria).
43	- NFR1: "p95 API latency under 300 ms" (docs/product/prd.md line 28, as cited in authoring-scope.md Analysis); G2 99.9% availability (prd.md line 17).
44	- Repo: `git ls-files` lists only src/shop/__init__.py and tests/test_health.py under code. Per authoring-scope.md Analysis, src has only `PAGE_SIZE`, `health()`, `list_customers()`; pyproject.toml has no dependencies. So there is no scheduler, worker, HTTP framework, persistence or carrier client. Any option adds its runtime from nothing; the question is which adds less.
45	
46	#### Option A: webhook push (preliminary winner)
47	How it works: each carrier POSTs a signed callback to one receiver route (proposed `POST /carriers/{carrier}/webhooks`). The handler reads the raw body, verifies the per-carrier HMAC and timestamp (d4, C-2), normalises the payload through a carrier adapter, writes the event and projection in one transaction (d2) and acks 2xx.
48	- AC-2: end-to-end latency is carrier send time plus our handler, typically seconds. Margin against 60 s is large. Carrier retry policy affects only failure cases (assumption A-D1-1 below).
49	- NFR1: handler does one HMAC check and one DB transaction, with no outbound calls (email is off-path per d3). This is bounded work, so p95 < 300 ms is plausible. Needs a load test (S5 in scope rollout).
50	- Simplicity: no scheduler, no per-order polling state, no carrier rate-limit management, no carrier credentials for outbound calls. Only a route and a verifier.
51	- Availability: carriers retry while we are down for short outages. Long outages leave status stale; no self-healing (see Option C).
52	- Security: public inbound endpoint. Needs raw-body HMAC, replay window, constant-time compare, body-size cap, rate limit.
53	- Cons: duplicates and out-of-order delivery need idempotency (unique carrier + carrier_event_id, occurred_at comparison, d2).
54	
55	#### Option B: status API polling
56	How it works: a scheduled job iterates open shipments per carrier, calls the carrier status API, diffs against the stored status and records changes.
57	- AC-2: worst-case latency is roughly poll interval + call duration + processing. To keep a safety margin under 60 s the interval must be about 30 s or less. Each open shipment is then polled about twice a minute per carrier, unless a carrier offers a bulk or since-cursor endpoint (unverified, assumption A-D1-2). Call volume grows linearly with open orders; rate limits and per-call costs are unknown.
58	- NFR1: the poller is not on a user-facing request path, so p95 of shopper endpoints is not directly affected. It does compete for DB and CPU with them.
59	- Simplicity: no inbound surface and no signature handling, but needs a scheduler/worker process, outbound carrier credentials, rate-limit and backoff logic and per-carrier clients. None of this exists in src.
60	- Availability: self-healing after our downtime (next poll catches up). But a carrier API outage stalls ingestion, and a long poll cycle can itself breach AC-2.
61	- Cons: wasted calls when nothing changed; more infra; tight coupling of AC-2 to cron cadence.
62	
63	#### Option C: hybrid (webhook primary plus low-frequency reconciliation poll)
64	How it works: Option A plus a slow poll (for example every 5-15 min, only for open shipments with no recent event) to repair missed callbacks.
65	- Pros: closes the missed-callback gap and the long-outage availability concern against G2.
66	- Cons: needs everything Option B needs (scheduler, outbound clients, credentials) in addition to Option A, so it is strictly more than the simplest option. Fails C-1 "simplest" for the first release.
67	- Disposition: rejected for release 1, recorded as optional follow-up slice S6. It can share the outbox drain loop slot from d3 as the first background process, so adding it later is additive and does not change the handler or data model (event dedupe key makes polled and pushed events converge).
68	
69	#### Recommendation
70	Option A. It is the simplest option that meets AC-2 with margin and NFR1 (C-1), requires no new scheduling infrastructure and authenticates with a per-carrier shared secret as C-2 allows. Option C stays as a documented, additive follow-up; the main residual risk (missed callbacks) is mitigated by carrier retries, an idempotent handler, and a stale-open-shipment alert.
71

73	- A-D1-1: both carriers retry non-2xx callbacks with backoff for a bounded window. Not verified; confirm in carrier docs when building the adapters (consistent with authoring-scope A-2).
74	- A-D1-2: carrier polling APIs have no bulk/since-cursor guarantee, so per-shipment polling cost is assumed for Option B. If a bulk endpoint exists, Option B's cost drops but infra need remains.
75	- A-D1-3: p95 < 300 ms applies to the webhook receiver as an API endpoint; the handler budget is verify + one transaction. Verified by load test, not by this design.

80	### d2 Status data model (research slice; refines scope notes d2, authoring-scope.md lines 19-22)
81	
82	Drivers: AC-1 (current status AND history per order, requirements.md "Acceptance criteria"); idempotency and out-of-order carrier callbacks (d1 picks webhook push, so carriers retry and reorder; authoring-scope.md line 14); NFR1 p95 < 300 ms (docs/product/prd.md:28, as cited in scope notes line 5); AC-3 needs one email per status change, with an outbox row written in the same transaction (d3, scope line 26). Code evidence: src/shop/__init__.py (lines 1-9 per scope notes) has no persistence and no order model, so every option is greenfield and the orders table is owned by checkout (F2); the design only adds a FK to it (assumption A-5, scope line 90).
83	
84	#### Option A: append-only event table + orders.current_status projection, same transaction (recommended)
85	- How it works: `order_status_event(id, order_id FK, carrier, carrier_event_id, status, occurred_at, received_at, raw_payload_ref)`, UNIQUE(carrier, carrier_event_id), INDEX(order_id, occurred_at). `orders` gains `current_status` and `current_status_at`. Handler, in one transaction: INSERT event ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING; if 0 rows inserted it is a duplicate, so commit and ack 200 with no further effect (no second email). Otherwise UPDATE orders SET current_status, current_status_at WHERE id = ? AND (current_status_at IS NULL OR current_status_at < :occurred_at) (tie-break on event id); and INSERT email_outbox keyed by event id. The email decision is made on the status change event, not on projection movement (see Open questions Q1).
86	- Idempotency: DB-enforced via the unique key, so concurrent duplicate deliveries are safe without locks.
87	- Out-of-order: late event is still stored (history complete, AC-1) but cannot regress the projection, since the guarded UPDATE is conditional on occurred_at. History reads order by occurred_at, not received_at.
88	- AC-1: history = `SELECT ... WHERE order_id=? ORDER BY occurred_at`; current status = single column read. Order list page reads orders.current_status with no join, which protects NFR1 on list views.
89	- NFR1: write path is 1 INSERT + 1 conditional UPDATE + 1 outbox INSERT in one local transaction, no outbound calls: well under 300 ms.
90	- Cons: two sources of truth; projection can drift if any code path writes events without the projection. Mitigation: a single repository function is the only writer (module src/shop/tracking/), plus a consistency check query (current_status equals latest event) in tests and an ops job; projection is rebuildable from events at any time.
91	- Cost: storage grows by a few rows per order (6 normalised statuses, scope A-4); negligible.
92	
93	#### Option B: derive-on-read, events only (no projection)
94	- How it works: same event table and unique key; current status = latest event by occurred_at (`ORDER BY occurred_at DESC LIMIT 1`, or a lateral join for lists). No orders column.
95	- Pros: one write, no drift by construction, nothing to rebuild; idempotency and history identical to A.
96	- Cons: every order list needs a latest-per-order lookup; with the (order_id, occurred_at) index this is cheap for one order but a per-row lateral join on a page of orders is a larger NFR1 risk and couples checkout/order queries to the tracking table. The "did status change" decision for AC-3 needs a read of the previous latest event inside the transaction (a lock or serialisable read is needed to avoid two concurrent callbacks both deciding they changed it). Marginally weaker under concurrency than A's conditional UPDATE.
97	- Viability: genuinely viable at small scale; scale is not quantified in the PRD (assumption, see Risks).
98	
99	#### Option C: single mutable orders.status column, overwritten
100	- How it works: callback overwrites the column.
101	- Fails AC-1 (no history) and has no dedupe key, so duplicates cannot be told from changes (AC-3 would double-send), and an out-of-order callback regresses the status. Rejected as non-viable against requirements; listed for completeness, not a strawman for the choice between A and B.
102	
103	#### Option D (variant of A, noted): materialised view or cache of the latest event instead of a column
104	- Rejected: adds refresh lag against AC-2 and operational complexity for no gain over a column updated in-transaction.
105	
106	### Preliminary recommendation
107	Option A. It meets AC-1 with a trivial history query, gives DB-enforced idempotency, handles out-of-order without losing data, keeps list reads flat for NFR1, and the projection is always rebuildable from the log, which removes most of its drift risk. Fall back to Option B only if the team wants to avoid adding columns to the checkout-owned orders table (see Q2); the event table and handler contract are identical, so the switch is cheap.

110	### d3 Email on every status change (AC-3): synchronous vs transactional outbox vs fire-and-forget
111	
112	Evidence read: requirements.md (AC-3 "emailed on every order status change"; prompt answer 3: outbound transactional email API, provider undecided, does not change the design); authoring-scope.md d1-d3 and NFR checklist (NFR1 p95 < 300 ms from docs/product/prd.md:28 as cited there; G2 99.9%, prd.md:17); code reality per scope notes (src/shop/__init__.py lines 1-9: no framework, no persistence, no email, no background process; pyproject.toml has no dependencies). I did not re-open the PRD or src files in this slice; those citations are inherited from the scope notes.
113	
114	Constraints that frame the choice:
115	- AC-3 says "every" status change: a lost email is a requirement violation, so the delivery guarantee must be at-least-once with dedupe, not best-effort.
116	- NFR1 p95 < 300 ms applies to the webhook handler (d1 pick A) and the shopper endpoints. Handler is meant to be verify + one DB transaction (scope d1). A third-party call inside it puts provider latency into the p95.
117	- C-3: provider unknown, so the design needs a provider-agnostic `EmailSender` port.
118	- Carriers retry on non-2xx or timeout (assumption A-6 below). A handler that blocks on or fails because of the email API turns a mail outage into duplicate carrier callbacks.
119	- Operability: shop has no background process today and no deployment view (scope Architecture conformance call), so any new worker is new infra.
120	
121	#### Option A: synchronous send inside the webhook handler
122	How it works: after verifying and persisting the event, the handler calls `EmailSender.send()` and only then returns 2xx.
123	- Pros: fewest moving parts, no worker, no extra table; email is sent at once.
124	- Cons: provider latency adds directly to handler latency, so NFR1 p95 depends on a third party (typical transactional APIs are 100-500 ms per call, an assumption, not measured here, so one call alone can exceed the 300 ms budget). Provider failure forces a choice: fail the callback (carrier retries, duplicates, the event is already committed so dedupe must absorb it, and the email is still not guaranteed) or swallow the error (email lost, violating AC-3). Cannot retry with backoff without holding the carrier connection. Couples availability (G2) of ingestion to the email provider.
125	- Verdict: fails NFR1 risk and AC-3 reliability. Viable only as a prototype.
126	
127	#### Option B: transactional outbox with an async sender
128	How it works: in the same DB transaction that inserts the `order_status_event` and moves `orders.current_status`, the handler inserts one `email_outbox` row (columns proposed: id, event_id UNIQUE, order_id, recipient reference, status in pending/sent/failed/dead, attempts, next_attempt_at, created_at, sent_at, last_error). The handler returns 2xx after commit with no outbound call. A sender drains rows `WHERE status='pending' AND next_attempt_at <= now()` (claimed with row locking, e.g. `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, or an equivalent atomic claim, depending on the DB chosen, A-1), calls `EmailSender.send(idempotency_key=event_id)`, and marks sent; on error it increments attempts and sets `next_attempt_at` with exponential backoff, moving to `dead` after a cap (alerted).
129	- Pros: handler stays DB-only, protecting NFR1; the email intent is committed atomically with the status change, so no status change can exist without a pending email (AC-3 "every"); retries survive crashes and provider outages; unique(event_id) plus the provider idempotency key gives effectively-once sending; unique(event_id) also makes a duplicate carrier callback (already deduped on carrier_event_id in d2) unable to enqueue a second email; adds natural metrics (outbox depth, oldest pending age). The same drain loop can later host the reconciliation poll (scope d1 option C).
130	- Cons: new background component; one more table; delivery latency is the drain interval plus send time (poll interval proposal 1-5 s, or wake-on-insert signal, so email lands well within a minute; this is a proposed internal target, not a requirement); at-least-once means a crash between provider accept and `mark sent` can double-send unless the provider honours the idempotency key (assumption A-7), otherwise a rare duplicate email is accepted.
131	- Sub-choice B1, in-process drain loop (thread/async task started with the app): simplest deploy, no new process type; with several app replicas it needs the row-claim lock above, and a stuck app stops sending. Sub-choice B2, separate worker process: independent scaling and failure isolation, but needs a second deployable that deployment docs do not define yet. Recommendation: build the drain as a plain function `drain_once()` behind the `EmailSender` port, run in-process (B1) for the first release, and move to B2 later without changing tables or the port. Wrong-decision cost is small.
132	
133	#### Option C: in-process fire-and-forget after commit
134	How it works: after commit, the handler enqueues the send onto an in-memory queue or spawns a thread, and returns immediately.
135	- Pros: handler fast, no table, no polling loop.
136	- Cons: the queue is lost on crash, deploy or restart, and nothing records that an email was owed, so there is no way to detect or repair a miss; no durable retry; violates AC-3 "every"; harder to observe. The gap between commit and enqueue is itself a loss window.
137	- Verdict: rejected. Cheaper than B only until the first deploy mid-send.
138	
139	#### Comparison against criteria
140	| Criterion | A sync | B outbox | C fire-and-forget |
141	|---|---|---|---|
142	| AC-3 every change emailed | no (lossy or duplicate-prone) | yes (durable, retried) | no (lossy) |
143	| NFR1 p95 < 300 ms | at risk (provider in path) | protected | protected |
144	| Failure isolation from provider (G2) | none | full | partial |
145	| Operability (visibility of backlog) | none | outbox depth/age, dead letters | none |
146	| New infra | none | drain loop, one table | thread/queue |
147	
148	Recommendation: Option B with B1 first. Consistent with the scope notes' preliminary pick.
149	
150	#### Design details the draft should carry for B (so the LLD owners get a precise input; not LLD redesign)
151	- Trigger rule: write an outbox row only when the event actually changes `orders.current_status` (the projection moves). A duplicate or older out-of-order event (ignored per d2) creates no email; this is the reading of "every status change" I assume (A-8). History-only late events do not notify.
152	- Content: email carries order reference, new status, timestamp, link to the order status page; no secrets, minimal PII (recipient resolved at send time from the order, stored by reference not copied into the outbox, to avoid a second PII copy; the port receives the address only for the call).
153	- Rendering: template per status chosen at send time from the status enum (A-4).
154	- Failure policy: retry with exponential backoff and jitter (proposal: 1 min doubling, cap about 1 h, max about 8 attempts, then `dead` plus an alert); permanent 4xx (bad address) goes to `dead` without further retries; 429/5xx/timeouts retry.
155	- Ordering: emails for one order should be sent in event order; drain by `created_at` per order and do not send event N+1 before N is terminal, or accept occasional reorder (A-9, minor; recommend simple per-order ordering because stale-looking emails confuse shoppers).
156	- Metrics: outbox pending count, oldest pending age, sends ok/failed/dead, send latency; alert on oldest pending age above a threshold (proposal 5 min) and any `dead` row.
157	- Retention: purge `sent` rows after a retention window (proposal 30 days) to bound table size.
158	- Test seams (NFR2 >= 90%): `EmailSender` port with a fake; `drain_once(now)` takes a clock, so backoff and dead-letter paths are unit-testable without sleeping.
159	- Feature flag: sending can be gated by `order_tracking_enabled` (scope Risks), while outbox rows are still written, so enabling later flushes nothing stale: add a rule that rows older than a cutoff are dropped, not sent, on first enable (open point, see Open questions).

164	### d4 Callback authentication for carrier webhooks (settled input: C-2 callbacks authenticated, shared secret per carrier acceptable; requirements.md Prompt item 2)
165	
166	Evidence read: requirements.md (Prompt items 1-2: both carriers "support signed webhook push"; AC-2 within a minute); authoring-scope.md (## Decisions d4 lines 30-33, NFR checklist Security line 37, d2 unique (carrier, carrier_event_id) line 20, Risks "Secret leakage/rotation" line 97, A-2 line 90). Code reality from scope notes: src/shop/__init__.py lines 1-9 is a stub and pyproject.toml has no dependencies, so any option should use the Python standard library only (`hmac`, `hashlib`, `secrets`); I did not re-open src in this slice.
167	
168	Shared facts for both options:
169	- Endpoint is `POST /carriers/{carrier}/webhooks` (scope d1 option A). The `{carrier}` path segment selects which secret to use; an unknown carrier gets 404 with no secret lookup.
170	- Failure response is a uniform 401 that does not reveal which check failed (scope NFR Security line 37). Verification runs BEFORE any parsing or DB write, so an unauthenticated caller costs one HMAC/compare, and the NFR1 p95 < 300 ms budget (prd.md:28 per scope line 5) is not at risk.
171	- Replay: d2 already makes the handler idempotent via unique (carrier, carrier_event_id), so a replayed valid body creates no second event and no second email (d3 outbox row is written in the same transaction). The auth layer therefore only needs to bound replay, not eliminate it.
172	
173	#### Option A: HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body plus timestamp (recommended)
174	How it works: carrier sends `X-Signature` (hex or base64 HMAC-SHA256) and `X-Timestamp`. Shop computes HMAC over `timestamp + "." + raw_body` with the carrier's secret, compares with `hmac.compare_digest`, and rejects when |now - timestamp| exceeds a tolerance (proposed 5 minutes, configurable). Raw bytes must be captured before JSON parsing. Rotation: each carrier has an ordered list of at most two secrets (current, previous); verification tries both, so the carrier can switch on its own schedule; remove the previous secret after the overlap window.
175	Pros: secret never on the wire; body integrity (tampering of status, order or tracking number is detected); replay bounded by the timestamp window and made harmless by d2 dedupe; matches the brief that both carriers "support signed webhook push", so no carrier-side extra work; stdlib only, so no new dependency; rotation without downtime.
176	Cons: raw-body access is needed (framework choice is undecided, A-1; must be a requirement on the HTTP layer); depends on carrier signature scheme (exact header names, encoding, whether timestamp is signed; A-2); clock skew between carrier and shop can cause false rejects (mitigated by tolerance and NTP); a carrier that re-sends retries with the ORIGINAL timestamp could be rejected after the window, losing events (see Risks).
177	Implementation cost: low-moderate; one pure function `verify_signature(secret_list, headers, raw_body, now)` per carrier adapter, trivially unit-testable (supports NFR2 >= 90%, scope line 40).
178	
179	#### Option B: static shared token in a header, constant-time compare
180	How it works: carrier sends `Authorization: Bearer <token>` or `X-Carrier-Token`; shop compares against the per-carrier token with `hmac.compare_digest` over TLS. Rotation: accept current+previous token.
181	Pros: simplest to build and to configure on the carrier side; no raw-body capture, no clock dependency; works even if a carrier's signing is awkward.
182	Cons: the secret is sent on every request, so any TLS-terminating proxy, access log or APM tool that captures headers leaks it (scope Security line 37 already forbids logging secrets, which is harder to enforce for headers); no integrity (a valid token authorises any body); fully replayable by anyone who observes one request, so replay is limited only by d2 dedupe, and a captured token allows forging NEW events with fresh event ids; does not use the signed push capability the carriers already offer.
183	Implementation cost: lowest, but the saving over A is small (about one function), so it does not buy much.
184	
185	#### Option C (considered, not a standalone choice): network controls only (mTLS or carrier IP allowlist)
186	Stronger transport identity if both carriers offer mTLS or fixed egress IPs, but this is unconfirmed (no source says so), adds certificate or ingress operations that do not exist (no hld/deployment.md per scope line 45), and does not satisfy C-2's "shared secret per carrier" framing. Recorded as an optional defence-in-depth layer at the edge, not as the application-level decision.
187	
188	#### Comparison against criteria
189	| Criterion | A: HMAC + timestamp | B: static token |
190	|---|---|---|
191	| Security (C-2, NFR) | Authenticity + integrity, secret not sent | Authenticity only, secret sent each call |
192	| Replay | Bounded by window, harmless via d2 | Unbounded, only d2 dedupe |
193	| Rotation | Current+previous secret overlap | Current+previous token overlap |
194	| Compromise via logs/proxy | Signature is single-use-ish, secret not exposed | Token exposed, forgery possible |
195	| Implementation cost | Low-moderate, stdlib | Lowest, stdlib |
196	| Dependency on carrier | Needs signed push (stated available) | Needs custom header support (assumed) |
197	| Perf impact (NFR1) | One HMAC over small body, negligible | Negligible |
198	
199	#### Recommendation for d4
200	Option A. B loses on the security NFR for a marginal saving, and the carriers' signed push is stated as available (requirements.md Prompt item 1). Concrete parameters to put in the draft: per-carrier secret list in env/secret store (never in repo or logs), constant-time compare, 5-minute tolerance (proposal, tunable), uniform 401, 64 KiB body cap checked before hashing (proposal), metrics `callbacks_rejected{reason}` with the reason kept in metrics/internal logs only, not in the response. Fall back to B only for a carrier that proves unable to sign, as a per-carrier adapter setting, and then require TLS plus the edge controls from Option C; that fallback is itself a risk acceptance for the team to note at review.
201	
202	Assumptions (flagged, user cannot answer; confirm in the carrier adapter slice S3):
203	- A-2 (carried from scope): exact header names, digest encoding, signed string layout and timestamp semantics per carrier come from carrier docs, not from anything in the repo.
204	- A-d4-1: carriers re-sign each retry with a fresh timestamp. If a carrier retries with the original timestamp, set the tolerance above its maximum retry horizon, because d2 idempotency makes a wide window safe.
205	- A-d4-2: each carrier can hold two secrets or can switch at an agreed time, so overlap-based rotation works; if not, rotation needs a short agreed maintenance window.
206	- A-d4-3: the HTTP layer (undecided, A-1) can expose the unparsed request body.

316	- Public inbound endpoint is an attack surface. Mitigation: per-carrier HMAC with timestamp window, constant-time compare, 401 without detail, body-size cap, rate limit, no secret/signature logging, rotation by accepting current+previous secret.

324	- Timestamp ties or clock skew from carriers: equal or skewed occurred_at could pick the wrong "latest". Mitigation: tie-break by event id/received_at; use history ordering by (occurred_at, id); log projections that did not move for diagnosis.
325	- Row contention on a hot order (concurrent callbacks): the conditional UPDATE serialises per order row; acceptable at per-order rates (a handful of events per order).
326	- Dependency on checkout-owned orders table (Q2): schema coordination; blast radius is one migration touching a table that does not yet exist in code (src/shop/__init__.py has no persistence).
327	- Unknown scale (volume of orders and events not in the PRD as read in scope notes): assumed modest; Option B's list-read cost and Option A's write amplification would both be re-checked in the S5 load test against NFR1.
328	- Raw payload retention may include personal data (shipping address): store a reference or minimised payload only (scope NFR checklist, compliance note line 39).
329	- Backfill: orders existing before rollout have no events; S1 seeds one event per order from its current known state, or leaves history empty with current_status null (displayed as "processing"); decide at S1.

339	- Provider outage visibility: with the outbox the failure is silent to the shopper unless alerts exist; S5 observability must ship before the flag goes on.

341	- Reviewer checks for d3: the handler makes no outbound call; outbox insert is in the same transaction as the event and projection; unique(event_id); trigger rule A-8 stated; retry and dead-letter policy stated; provider stays behind the port (C-3); both rejected options have explicit cons.

9	# Tech design — EVAL-1: Order tracking
10	
11	## Decision & options
12	
13	Decision: receive carrier status changes by signed webhook push (HMAC-SHA256 per carrier secret), store them as an append-only event history with an in-transaction `orders.current_status` projection, and send shopper emails from a transactional outbox drained off the request path behind a provider-agnostic `EmailSender` port.
14	
15	### Context
16	
17	- Problem: shoppers must track an order from payment to delivery: status and history (AC-1), carrier changes reaching the shop within a minute (AC-2), and an email on every status change (AC-3). Feature PRD R1-R3 (`docs/product/features/order-tracking/prd.md` lines 13-15), product feature F3, supports G1.
18	- Scope: epic-level design. Child slices are laid out in Rollout & migration, and no child tickets are created now (C-4).
19	- Binding constraints: NFR1 p95 API latency under 300 ms and NFR2 coverage at least 90% (`docs/product/prd.md` NFR section), G2 99.9% availability.
20	- Codebase reality: `src/shop/__init__.py` has only `PAGE_SIZE`, `health()` and `list_customers()`. `pyproject.toml` lists no dependencies. There is no HTTP framework, persistence, order model, scheduler, email or carrier code. The design is greenfield and names modules (`src/shop/tracking/`) and contracts, not libraries (A-1).
21	- Settled decisions (clarification ledger):
22	  - C-1: weigh webhook against polling and pick the simplest option that meets p95 < 300 ms.
23	  - C-2: carrier callbacks are authenticated, and a shared secret per carrier is acceptable.
24	  - C-3: email goes through an outbound transactional email API. The provider is undecided and does not change the design.
25	  - C-4: the epic is fanned out later, so child slices are planned in the rollout and no tickets are created.
26	- Assumptions: A-1 to A-5 are listed under Open questions.
27	
28	```mermaid
29	flowchart LR
30	  carrier["Carrier A / B"] -->|"signed webhook"| rx["Webhook receiver"]
31	  rx -->|"one transaction"| db[("order_status_event, orders.current_status, email_outbox")]
32	  db --> drain["Outbox drain (EmailSender port)"]
33	  drain --> mail["Transactional email API"]
34	  shopper["Shopper"] -->|"status and history"| api["Shopper read API"]
35	  api --> db
36	```
37	
38	### Options considered
39	
40	#### Decision d1: carrier status ingestion
41	
42	##### Option A: webhook push (chosen)
43	Each carrier POSTs a signed callback to one receiver route. The handler verifies, normalises through a carrier adapter, writes in one transaction and acks.
44	- Pros: latency is seconds, so AC-2 has a large margin. There is no scheduler, polling state or rate-limit exposure. The handler is one signature check plus one transaction with no outbound calls, so p95 < 300 ms is plausible (to be proven by the S5 load test).
45	- Cons: public inbound surface, needs idempotency for duplicate and reordered deliveries, and missed callbacks during our downtime are not self-healing.
46	
47	##### Option B: status API polling
48	A scheduled job polls each carrier for all open shipments.
49	- AC-2 forces an interval of about 30 s or less (worst case is interval plus call time), so each open shipment is polled about twice a minute per carrier. Cost and rate-limit risk grow with open orders (bulk endpoints are unverified, A-D1-2).
50	- Needs a scheduler or worker, outbound credentials and per-carrier clients, none of which exist. It self-heals after downtime but a carrier API outage stalls ingestion.
51	
52	##### Option C: hybrid (webhook plus slow reconciliation poll)
53	Closes the missed-callback gap but needs everything Option B needs on top of Option A, so it is not the simplest (C-1). It is rejected for release 1 and kept as the additive follow-up S6.
54	
55	#### Decision d2: status data model
56	
57	##### Option A: append-only `order_status_event` plus `orders.current_status` projection in the same transaction (chosen)
58	- Mechanics:
59	  - The table is UNIQUE(carrier, carrier_event_id) with INDEX(order_id, occurred_at).
60	  - The handler runs INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. A conflict means a duplicate, so it acks with no further effect.
61	  - Otherwise it runs an UPDATE of `orders` guarded by `current_status_at < occurred_at`, plus an `email_outbox` insert only when the projection moved.
62	- Pros:
63	  - History is a plain ordered query (AC-1).
64	  - Idempotency is enforced by the database without locks.
65	  - A late event is stored but cannot regress the projection.
66	  - List pages read one column with no join, which protects NFR1.
67	  - The projection is rebuildable from events.
68	- Cons: two sources of truth. Mitigation: a single writer function, an invariant test and a rebuild script.
69	
70	##### Option B: events only, derive the current status on read
71	- Pros: one write and no drift.
72	- Cons: lists need a latest-per-order lateral join (an NFR1 risk), and the "did status change" decision for AC-3 needs a lock or serialisable read. It is viable at small scale and is the fallback if the team does not want columns added to the checkout-owned `orders` table. The event table and handler contract are identical, so switching is cheap.
73	
74	##### Option C: single mutable `orders.status` column
75	Fails AC-1 (no history), has no dedupe key and regresses on out-of-order callbacks. It is not viable against the requirements and is listed for completeness only.
76	
77	#### Decision d3: email on every status change
78	
79	##### Option A: synchronous send inside the webhook handler
80	- Pros: simplest, with no worker.
81	- Cons: provider latency lands in the handler p95 (NFR1 at risk) and couples ingestion availability (G2) to the provider. Failing the callback causes carrier retries and duplicates, and swallowing the error loses the email (violates AC-3). Rejected.
82	
83	##### Option B: transactional outbox with an async sender (chosen)
84	- The handler inserts an `email_outbox` row (unique `event_id`) in the same transaction and returns. A `drain_once(now)` function claims pending rows atomically, calls `EmailSender.send(idempotency_key=event_id)` and retries with exponential backoff, moving to `dead` after a cap.
85	- Pros:
86	  - No status change can exist without a pending email.
87	  - The handler stays DB-only.
88	  - Retries survive crashes and provider outages.
89	  - Backlog age and depth are observable.
90	  - The provider stays behind the port (C-3).
91	- Cons: a new background component and one more table. A crash between provider accept and `mark sent` can double-send unless the provider honours the idempotency key (A-7).
92	- Hosting sub-choice: in-process drain loop first (B1), separate worker later (B2). Tables and the port do not change between them.
93	
94	##### Option C: in-process fire-and-forget after commit
95	Nothing records that an email was owed, so a crash or deploy loses mail, which violates "every". Rejected.
96	
97	#### Decision d4: callback authentication (C-2)
98	
99	##### Option A: HMAC-SHA256 over timestamp plus raw body, per-carrier secret (chosen)
100	- Mechanics:
101	  - Compare with `hmac.compare_digest`.
102	  - Tolerance of 5 minutes (proposal, configurable).
103	  - Rotation by accepting a current and a previous secret.
104	  - Verification runs before parsing or any DB write.
105	  - Uniform 401 with no detail.
106	  - Body cap of 64 KiB (proposal).
107	- Pros:
108	  - The secret never travels on the wire.
109	  - Body integrity.
110	  - Replay is bounded by the window and made harmless by the d2 unique key.
111	  - Standard library only.
112	  - Both carriers support signed push.
113	- Cons: needs raw-body access from the HTTP layer (A-1), depends on carrier scheme details (A-2), and clock skew or retries carrying the original timestamp can cause false rejects.
114	
115	##### Option B: static shared token in a header
116	- Pros: simplest, with no raw-body or clock dependency.
117	- Cons: the secret is sent on every request and can leak via proxy or access logs, there is no integrity, and a captured token allows forging new events. The saving over A is about one function.
118	- Kept only as a per-carrier fallback if a carrier cannot sign. That needs explicit team risk acceptance.
119	
120	##### Option C: network controls only (mTLS or IP allowlist)
121	Unconfirmed carrier support, no deployment view, and it does not match C-2. Recorded as optional edge defence-in-depth.
122	
123	```mermaid
124	sequenceDiagram
125	  participant C as Carrier
126	  participant R as Webhook receiver
127	  participant D as Database
128	  participant S as Outbox drain
129	  participant M as Email API
130	  C->>R: POST /carriers/{carrier}/webhooks (signed)
131	  R->>R: verify HMAC and timestamp, then normalise
132	  R->>D: one transaction: event, projection, outbox row
133	  R-->>C: 2xx
134	  S->>D: claim pending outbox rows
135	  S->>M: send (idempotency key = event id)
136	  S->>D: mark sent or schedule retry
137	```
138	
139	### Rationale
140	
141	- d1: webhook push is the simplest option meeting AC-2 with margin and NFR1 (C-1). Polling adds a scheduler, outbound credentials and per-shipment cost to hit a one-minute target. The hybrid is strictly more, so it is deferred as S6.
142	- d2: the event log with a projection gives AC-1 history, database-enforced idempotency and flat list reads. Derive-on-read is the cheap fallback.
143	- d3: AC-3 says "every", so durable at-least-once delivery with dedupe is required. The outbox also protects the NFR1 handler budget and decouples ingestion from the provider (C-3).
144	- d4: C-2 allows a shared secret, and HMAC is that secret used safely. The brief says both carriers already support signed push, so the extra security costs almost nothing.
145	- Email trigger rule: an email is sent only when `current_status` actually changes. Duplicates and stale out-of-order events are stored in history but do not email (A-8).
146	
147	### Decision records
148	
149	ADR text is written by /acs:docs-sync under `docs/architecture/adr` (/acs:code no longer authors ADRs). Accepted decisions:
150	- ADR: Ingest carrier status via signed webhook push (reconciliation poll deferred) (C-1).
151	- ADR: Order status history as append-only events with an in-transaction current-status projection.
152	- ADR: Shopper emails through a transactional outbox and an `EmailSender` port, with the provider left open (C-3).
153	- ADR: Authenticate carrier callbacks with per-carrier HMAC-SHA256 and a timestamp window (C-2).

211	## NFRs
212	
213	- **Security (required)**
214	  - Callbacks are authenticated by HMAC over the raw body with a timestamp window and a constant-time compare. Verification runs first, with a uniform 401 and the reason kept in metrics only.
215	  - Secrets are held per carrier in the environment or a secret store, never in the repo or logs. Rotation accepts the current and previous secret.
216	  - The public endpoint has a 64 KiB body cap and edge rate limiting (S5), and is TLS only.
217	  - Shopper endpoints return only the caller's own orders. The shopper authentication mechanism is undefined (A-3).
218	  - PII: the recipient is resolved at send time and passed only to the email provider. The outbox stores a reference, and `last_error` is scrubbed. Raw payloads are stored minimised or by reference.
219	- **Performance (required)**
220	  - NFR1: webhook p95 < 300 ms. The handler budget is one HMAC, one transaction (insert, conditional update, outbox insert) and no outbound calls.
221	  - Shopper status and history endpoints are also held to p95 < 300 ms. They are served by the (order_id, occurred_at) index and a flat `current_status` column. The S5 load test proves both.
222	  - AC-2: push latency is seconds against a 60 s target.
223	  - Internal proposal, not a requirement: outbox delivery delay p95 under 1 minute, with a drain interval of 1-5 s.
224	- **Availability** (G2 99.9%): carrier retries cover short outages. Long outages are covered later by S6. Alert on open shipments with no event beyond a threshold.
225	- **Operability**: metrics for callbacks received, rejected and duplicate, outbox depth, oldest pending age, sends ok/failed/dead, and send latency. Alert on any `dead` row.
226	- **Reliability**: the handler and sender are idempotent, with exponential backoff and a max of about 8 attempts (proposal).
227	- **Cost**: no polling cost. One email per status change.
228	- **Compliance**: shopper email is personal data. The PRD is silent, so the design applies minimisation only.
229	- **Testability** (NFR2 at least 90%): the verifier, adapters and ordering logic are pure functions. The email port has a fake, and `drain_once` takes a clock.
230	
231	## Risks
232	
233	- Blast radius: new module `src/shop/tracking/`, three data changes, and one new public endpoint. The `orders` table is owned by checkout (F2). No existing code changes, since `src` holds only stubs. Affected components are checkout (F2), order management (F4) and the platform shopper authentication.
234	- Orders dependency (highest): no orders entity or checkout exists (roadmap Q4 checkout precedes Q1 tracking). Mitigation: S1 ships a minimal stub if `orders` is not ready.
235	- Missed callbacks (downtime, or carrier retry policy unknown, A-D1-1). Mitigation: carrier retries, idempotent handler, stale-shipment alert and S6. If retries are absent, S6 becomes required.
236	- Wrong signature assumption (A-2) would reject all genuine callbacks. Mitigation: per-carrier verifier, contract tests with carrier sample payloads, and a staging run before the flag is enabled.
237	- Timestamp window or clock skew rejects genuine retries. Mitigation: wide tolerance (safe because of dedupe), NTP, and an alert on timestamp rejects.
238	- Projection drift. Mitigation: a single writer, an invariant test and a rebuild script. Events remain the truth.
239	- Duplicate emails after a crash. Mitigation: unique event_id plus the provider idempotency key (A-7). A rare duplicate is accepted over a lost email.
240	- Multi-replica double claim of an outbox row. Mitigation: an atomic claim and a two-drain concurrency test.
241	- First background process in the repo, with no deployment view. The wrong choice costs only a refactor of the drain loop hosting.
242	- NFR1 is not proven by design. S5 must include the outbox insert in its load test. Order and event volumes are not in the PRD (assumed modest).
243	- Fallback to a static token for an unable-to-sign carrier weakens security and needs explicit risk acceptance.
244	
245	### Rollout & migration
246	
247	Child slices, each one reviewable PR with coverage at least 90% (NFR2). No tickets are created now (C-4). Order: S1, then S2 and S3 in parallel, then S4, then S5, with S6 optional.

252	  S1 --> S3["S3 webhook receiver"]
253	  S2 --> S4["S4 email sender"]
254	  S3 --> S4

258	
259	- **S1 Data and domain.**
260	  - Scope: migrations for `order_status_event`, `orders.current_status` and `email_outbox`; the status enum; ordering rules; the single projection writer.
261	  - AC: AC-1 base. Duplicate insert is a no-op, a stale event does not regress the projection, the projection equals the latest event, and unit tests cover the transitions.
262	  - Depends on the `orders` table (stub if F2 is not ready).
263	  - Backfill: existing orders get a seeded event or a null status shown as "processing". Decide at S1.
264	- **S2 Shopper read API.**
265	  - Scope: status and history endpoints with owner authorisation.
266	  - AC: AC-1. Another shopper's order is refused. History is ordered by occurred_at. Endpoint p95 is measured against NFR1.
267	- **S3 Carrier webhook receiver.**
268	  - Scope: per-carrier HMAC verification, adapters A and B, idempotent persistence in one transaction (including the outbox row), ack. Behind flag `order_tracking_enabled`.
269	  - AC: AC-2, R3. Unsigned, expired and wrong-secret requests get a uniform 401. Verification uses raw bytes, tested with odd whitespace and key order. Duplicates and out-of-order callbacks behave as in S1. The handler makes no outbound calls.
270	  - Depends on S1. Outbox rows accumulate harmlessly until S4.
271	- **S4 Email outbox sender.**
272	  - Scope: the `EmailSender` port, a provider adapter, `drain_once`, backoff and dead-letter, and the status templates.
273	  - AC: AC-3. One email per status change, none for duplicates or stale events, retries survive a provider outage, and a crash cannot lose a row.

277	  - AC: p95 < 300 ms on webhook and read endpoints, alerts for outbox age and dead rows, and staging verification with each carrier before the flag is enabled.
278	- **S6 (optional follow-up) Reconciliation poll.** A slow poll for open shipments with no recent event, sharing the drain slot. It is additive because event dedupe makes polled and pushed events converge.

286	## Open questions
287	
288	No question blocks the design. The user cannot answer, so the items below are recorded as `assumed` (assumptions are not clarification ledger entries) for the team to confirm or overrule at review.
289	
290	- A-1 (assumed): the HTTP framework and database are undecided (no tech-stack view, no dependencies). Options: pick them in S1/S3, or author `hld/tech-stack.md` first. Requirement on the choice: raw-body access and an atomic row claim.
291	- A-2 (assumed): carrier signature headers, digest encoding and timestamp semantics, retry behaviour (A-D1-1) and re-signing on retry (A-d4-1) are confirmed from carrier docs in S3.
292	- A-2b (assumed, d2 idempotency): carriers supply a stable event id and an occurred-at timestamp in the signed payload, because the dedupe key is UNIQUE(carrier, carrier_event_id) and ordering uses `occurred_at`. 38	### d1 Carrier status ingestion: webhook push vs status API polling vs hybrid
39	Settled input: C-1 (weigh both, pick the simplest meeting PRD p95 < 300 ms) and C-2 (shared secret per carrier), from the run prompt in requirements.md "Prompt" section, items (1) and (2). Both carriers support signed webhook push and status API polling (same source).

41	Evidence:
42	- AC-2: "Carrier status changes reach the shop within a minute of the carrier recording them" (requirements.md, Acceptance criteria).
43	- NFR1: "p95 API latency under 300 ms" (docs/product/prd.md line 28, as cited in authoring-scope.md Analysis); G2 99.9% availability (prd.md line 17).
44	- Repo: `git ls-files` lists only src/shop/__init__.py and tests/test_health.py under code. Per authoring-scope.md Analysis, src has only `PAGE_SIZE`, `health()`, `list_customers()`; pyproject.toml has no dependencies. So there is no scheduler, worker, HTTP framework, persistence or carrier client. Any option adds its runtime from nothing; the question is which adds less.
45	
46	#### Option A: webhook push (preliminary winner)
47	How it works: each carrier POSTs a signed callback to one receiver route (proposed `POST /carriers/{carrier}/webhooks`). The handler reads the raw body, verifies the per-carrier HMAC and timestamp (d4, C-2), normalises the payload through a carrier adapter, writes the event and projection in one transaction (d2) and acks 2xx.
48	- AC-2: end-to-end latency is carrier send time plus our handler, typically seconds. Margin against 60 s is large. Carrier retry policy affects only failure cases (assumption A-D1-1 below).
49	- NFR1: handler does one HMAC check and one DB transaction, with no outbound calls (email is off-path per d3). This is bounded work, so p95 < 300 ms is plausible. Needs a load test (S5 in scope rollout).
50	- Simplicity: no scheduler, no per-order polling state, no carrier rate-limit management, no carrier credentials for outbound calls. Only a route and a verifier.
51	- Availability: carriers retry while we are down for short outages. Long outages leave status stale; no self-healing (see Option C).
52	- Security: public inbound endpoint. Needs raw-body HMAC, replay window, constant-time compare, body-size cap, rate limit.
53	- Cons: duplicates and out-of-order delivery need idempotency (unique carrier + carrier_event_id, occurred_at comparison, d2).
54	
55	#### Option B: status API polling
56	How it works: a scheduled job iterates open shipments per carrier, calls the carrier status API, diffs against the stored status and records changes.
57	- AC-2: worst-case latency is roughly poll interval + call duration + processing. To keep a safety margin under 60 s the interval must be about 30 s or less. Each open shipment is then polled about twice a minute per carrier, unless a carrier offers a bulk or since-cursor endpoint (unverified, assumption A-D1-2). Call volume grows linearly with open orders; rate limits and per-call costs are unknown.
58	- NFR1: the poller is not on a user-facing request path, so p95 of shopper endpoints is not directly affected. It does compete for DB and CPU with them.
59	- Simplicity: no inbound surface and no signature handling, but needs a scheduler/worker process, outbound carrier credentials, rate-limit and backoff logic and per-carrier clients. None of this exists in src.
60	- Availability: self-healing after our downtime (next poll catches up). But a carrier API outage stalls ingestion, and a long poll cycle can itself breach AC-2.
61	- Cons: wasted calls when nothing changed; more infra; tight coupling of AC-2 to cron cadence.
62	
63	#### Option C: hybrid (webhook primary plus low-frequency reconciliation poll)
64	How it works: Option A plus a slow poll (for example every 5-15 min, only for open shipments with no recent event) to repair missed callbacks.
65	- Pros: closes the missed-callback gap and the long-outage availability concern against G2.
66	- Cons: needs everything Option B needs (scheduler, outbound clients, credentials) in addition to Option A, so it is strictly more than the simplest option. Fails C-1 "simplest" for the first release.
67	- Disposition: rejected for release 1, recorded as optional follow-up slice S6. It can share the outbox drain loop slot from d3 as the first background process, so adding it later is additive and does not change the handler or data model (event dedupe key makes polled and pushed events converge).
68	
69	#### Recommendation
70	Option A. It is the simplest option that meets AC-2 with margin and NFR1 (C-1), requires no new scheduling infrastructure and authenticates with a per-carrier shared secret as C-2 allows. Option C stays as a documented, additive follow-up; the main residual risk (missed callbacks) is mitigated by carrier retries, an idempotent handler, and a stale-open-shipment alert.

80	### d2 Status data model (research slice; refines scope notes d2, authoring-scope.md lines 19-22)
81	
82	Drivers: AC-1 (current status AND history per order, requirements.md "Acceptance criteria"); idempotency and out-of-order carrier callbacks (d1 picks webhook push, so carriers retry and reorder; authoring-scope.md line 14); NFR1 p95 < 300 ms (docs/product/prd.md:28, as cited in scope notes line 5); AC-3 needs one email per status change, with an outbox row written in the same transaction (d3, scope line 26). Code evidence: src/shop/__init__.py (lines 1-9 per scope notes) has no persistence and no order model, so every option is greenfield and the orders table is owned by checkout (F2); the design only adds a FK to it (assumption A-5, scope line 90).
83	
84	#### Option A: append-only event table + orders.current_status projection, same transaction (recommended)
85	- How it works: `order_status_event(id, order_id FK, carrier, carrier_event_id, status, occurred_at, received_at, raw_payload_ref)`, UNIQUE(carrier, carrier_event_id), INDEX(order_id, occurred_at). `orders` gains `current_status` and `current_status_at`. Handler, in one transaction: INSERT event ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING; if 0 rows inserted it is a duplicate, so commit and ack 200 with no further effect (no second email). Otherwise UPDATE orders SET current_status, current_status_at WHERE id = ? AND (current_status_at IS NULL OR current_status_at < :occurred_at) (tie-break on event id); and INSERT email_outbox keyed by event id. The email decision is made on the status change event, not on projection movement (see Open questions Q1).
86	- Idempotency: DB-enforced via the unique key, so concurrent duplicate deliveries are safe without locks.
87	- Out-of-order: late event is still stored (history complete, AC-1) but cannot regress the projection, since the guarded UPDATE is conditional on occurred_at. History reads order by occurred_at, not received_at.
88	- AC-1: history = `SELECT ... WHERE order_id=? ORDER BY occurred_at`; current status = single column read. Order list page reads orders.current_status with no join, which protects NFR1 on list views.
89	- NFR1: write path is 1 INSERT + 1 conditional UPDATE + 1 outbox INSERT in one local transaction, no outbound calls: well under 300 ms.
90	- Cons: two sources of truth; projection can drift if any code path writes events without the projection. Mitigation: a single repository function is the only writer (module src/shop/tracking/), plus a consistency check query (current_status equals latest event) in tests and an ops job; projection is rebuildable from events at any time.
91	- Cost: storage grows by a few rows per order (6 normalised statuses, scope A-4); negligible.
92	
93	#### Option B: derive-on-read, events only (no projection)
94	- How it works: same event table and unique key; current status = latest event by occurred_at (`ORDER BY occurred_at DESC LIMIT 1`, or a lateral join for lists). No orders column.
95	- Pros: one write, no drift by construction, nothing to rebuild; idempotency and history identical to A.
96	- Cons: every order list needs a latest-per-order lookup; with the (order_id, occurred_at) index this is cheap for one order but a per-row lateral join on a page of orders is a larger NFR1 risk and couples checkout/order queries to the tracking table. The "did status change" decision for AC-3 needs a read of the previous latest event inside the transaction (a lock or serialisable read is needed to avoid two concurrent callbacks both deciding they changed it). Marginally weaker under concurrency than A's conditional UPDATE.
97	- Viability: genuinely viable at small scale; scale is not quantified in the PRD (assumption, see Risks).
98	
99	#### Option C: single mutable orders.status column, overwritten
100	- How it works: callback overwrites the column.
101	- Fails AC-1 (no history) and has no dedupe key, so duplicates cannot be told from changes (AC-3 would double-send), and an out-of-order callback regresses the status. Rejected as non-viable against requirements; listed for completeness, not a strawman for the choice between A and B.
102	
103	#### Option D (variant of A, noted): materialised view or cache of the latest event instead of a column
104	- Rejected: adds refresh lag against AC-2 and operational complexity for no gain over a column updated in-transaction.

106	### Preliminary recommendation
107	Option A. It meets AC-1 with a trivial history query, gives DB-enforced idempotency, handles out-of-order without losing data, keeps list reads flat for NFR1, and the projection is always rebuildable from the log, which removes most of its drift risk. Fall back to Option B only if the team wants to avoid adding columns to the checkout-owned orders table (see Q2); the event table and handler contract are identical, so the switch is cheap.

110	### d3 Email on every status change (AC-3): synchronous vs transactional outbox vs fire-and-forget
111	
112	Evidence read: requirements.md (AC-3 "emailed on every order status change"; prompt answer 3: outbound transactional email API, provider undecided, does not change the design); authoring-scope.md d1-d3 and NFR checklist (NFR1 p95 < 300 ms from docs/product/prd.md:28 as cited there; G2 99.9%, prd.md:17); code reality per scope notes (src/shop/__init__.py lines 1-9: no framework, no persistence, no email, no background process; pyproject.toml has no dependencies). I did not re-open the PRD or src files in this slice; those citations are inherited from the scope notes.
113	
114	Constraints that frame the choice:
115	- AC-3 says "every" status change: a lost email is a requirement violation, so the delivery guarantee must be at-least-once with dedupe, not best-effort.
116	- NFR1 p95 < 300 ms applies to the webhook handler (d1 pick A) and the shopper endpoints. Handler is meant to be verify + one DB transaction (scope d1). A third-party call inside it puts provider latency into the p95.
117	- C-3: provider unknown, so the design needs a provider-agnostic `EmailSender` port.
118	- Carriers retry on non-2xx or timeout (assumption A-6 below). A handler that blocks on or fails because of the email API turns a mail outage into duplicate carrier callbacks.
119	- Operability: shop has no background process today and no deployment view (scope Architecture conformance call), so any new worker is new infra.
120	
121	#### Option A: synchronous send inside the webhook handler
122	How it works: after verifying and persisting the event, the handler calls `EmailSender.send()` and only then returns 2xx.
123	- Pros: fewest moving parts, no worker, no extra table; email is sent at once.
124	- Cons: provider latency adds directly to handler latency, so NFR1 p95 depends on a third party (typical transactional APIs are 100-500 ms per call, an assumption, not measured here, so one call alone can exceed the 300 ms budget). Provider failure forces a choice: fail the callback (carrier retries, duplicates, the event is already committed so dedupe must absorb it, and the email is still not guaranteed) or swallow the error (email lost, violating AC-3). Cannot retry with backoff without holding the carrier connection. Couples availability (G2) of ingestion to the email provider.
125	- Verdict: fails NFR1 risk and AC-3 reliability. Viable only as a prototype.
126	
127	#### Option B: transactional outbox with an async sender
128	How it works: in the same DB transaction that inserts the `order_status_event` and moves `orders.current_status`, the handler inserts one `email_outbox` row (columns proposed: id, event_id UNIQUE, order_id, recipient reference, status in pending/sent/failed/dead, attempts, next_attempt_at, created_at, sent_at, last_error). The handler returns 2xx after commit with no outbound call. A sender drains rows `WHERE status='pending' AND next_attempt_at <= now()` (claimed with row locking, e.g. `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, or an equivalent atomic claim, depending on the DB chosen, A-1), calls `EmailSender.send(idempotency_key=event_id)`, and marks sent; on error it increments attempts and sets `next_attempt_at` with exponential backoff, moving to `dead` after a cap (alerted).
129	- Pros: handler stays DB-only, protecting NFR1; the email intent is committed atomically with the status change, so no status change can exist without a pending email (AC-3 "every"); retries survive crashes and provider outages; unique(event_id) plus the provider idempotency key gives effectively-once sending; unique(event_id) also makes a duplicate carrier callback (already deduped on carrier_event_id in d2) unable to enqueue a second email; adds natural metrics (outbox depth, oldest pending age). The same drain loop can later host the reconciliation poll (scope d1 option C).
130	- Cons: new background component; one more table; delivery latency is the drain interval plus send time (poll interval proposal 1-5 s, or wake-on-insert signal, so email lands well within a minute; this is a proposed internal target, not a requirement); at-least-once means a crash between provider accept and `mark sent` can double-send unless the provider honours the idempotency key (assumption A-7), otherwise a rare duplicate email is accepted.
131	- Sub-choice B1, in-process drain loop (thread/async task started with the app): simplest deploy, no new process type; with several app replicas it needs the row-claim lock above, and a stuck app stops sending. Sub-choice B2, separate worker process: independent scaling and failure isolation, but needs a second deployable that deployment docs do not define yet. Recommendation: build the drain as a plain function `drain_once()` behind the `EmailSender` port, run in-process (B1) for the first release, and move to B2 later without changing tables or the port. Wrong-decision cost is small.
132	
133	#### Option C: in-process fire-and-forget after commit
134	How it works: after commit, the handler enqueues the send onto an in-memory queue or spawns a thread, and returns immediately.
135	- Pros: handler fast, no table, no polling loop.
136	- Cons: the queue is lost on crash, deploy or restart, and nothing records that an email was owed, so there is no way to detect or repair a miss; no durable retry; violates AC-3 "every"; harder to observe. The gap between commit and enqueue is itself a loss window.
137	- Verdict: rejected. Cheaper than B only until the first deploy mid-send.
138	
139	#### Comparison against criteria
140	| Criterion | A sync | B outbox | C fire-and-forget |
141	|---|---|---|---|
142	| AC-3 every change emailed | no (lossy or duplicate-prone) | yes (durable, retried) | no (lossy) |
143	| NFR1 p95 < 300 ms | at risk (provider in path) | protected | protected |
144	| Failure isolation from provider (G2) | none | full | partial |
145	| Operability (visibility of backlog) | none | outbox depth/age, dead letters | none |
146	| New infra | none | drain loop, one table | thread/queue |
147	
148	Recommendation: Option B with B1 first. Consistent with the scope notes' preliminary pick.
149	
150	#### Design details the draft should carry for B (so the LLD owners get a precise input; not LLD redesign)
151	- Trigger rule: write an outbox row only when the event actually changes `orders.current_status` (the projection moves). A duplicate or older out-of-order event (ignored per d2) creates no email; this is the reading of "every status change" I assume (A-8). History-only late events do not notify.
152	- Content: email carries order reference, new status, timestamp, link to the order status page; no secrets, minimal PII (recipient resolved at send time from the order, stored by reference not copied into the outbox, to avoid a second PII copy; the port receives the address only for the call).
153	- Rendering: template per status chosen at send time from the status enum (A-4).
154	- Failure policy: retry with exponential backoff and jitter (proposal: 1 min doubling, cap about 1 h, max about 8 attempts, then `dead` plus an alert); permanent 4xx (bad address) goes to `dead` without further retries; 429/5xx/timeouts retry.
155	- Ordering: emails for one order should be sent in event order; drain by `created_at` per order and do not send event N+1 before N is terminal, or accept occasional reorder (A-9, minor; recommend simple per-order ordering because stale-looking emails confuse shoppers).
156	- Metrics: outbox pending count, oldest pending age, sends ok/failed/dead, send latency; alert on oldest pending age above a threshold (proposal 5 min) and any `dead` row.
157	- Retention: purge `sent` rows after a retention window (proposal 30 days) to bound table size.
158	- Test seams (NFR2 >= 90%): `EmailSender` port with a fake; `drain_once(now)` takes a clock, so backoff and dead-letter paths are unit-testable without sleeping.
159	- Feature flag: sending can be gated by `order_tracking_enabled` (scope Risks), while outbox rows are still written, so enabling later flushes nothing stale: add a rule that rows older than a cutoff are dropped, not sent, on first enable (open point, see Open questions).
160	
161	Single-option check: three real alternatives exist, A and C are rejected on stated criteria, so this is not a single-option decision.
